### feedback_cross_language_pitfalls.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language design pitfalls
description: Three approaches the user rejected when designing SoraMech's cross-language wire format
type: feedback
originSessionId: e9ed70c7-2b63-425c-987c-6431040bedfb
---
When designing anything that touches the cross-language data path, avoid these three shapes — the user pushed back on each and the rejections are load-bearing for the architecture.

**1. Don't propose runtime "handles" that route operations back to the originating spec.**

**Why:** Real library functions in the wild (qsort, libcurl, anything from libc) expect actual native values — a real `int (*)(int,int)` function pointer, a real `char *` — not a SoraMech-issued id string. They can't be modified to participate in our runtime's routing scheme. The wire must carry data the destination spec can fully reconstruct into a native value, not opaque tokens.

**How to apply:** When a value seems hard to serialize (function pointers, coroutines, opaque pointers), decompose to data primitives (address + signature, bytecode + upvalues, ptr + length). If the destination needs a callable, the destination spec synthesizes one at reconstruction time (libffi trampoline for C, `ffi.cast` for LuaJIT). The "phone home" callback that the trampoline performs internally is fine — it's an artifact of the destination spec's reconstruction, not exposed in the wire format. What's forbidden is a wire primitive that says "operations on this value cross back to the source."

**2. Don't propose pair-wise language conversion paths (lua→c, c→lua, etc.).**

**Why:** N languages means N² conversion paths, which means adding a new language breaks the existing ones. The wire must use a language-agnostic intermediate (JSON) and every spec must implement only the two pair-symmetric callbacks (`to_json`, `from_json`). New language = implement those two functions, nothing else touches.

**How to apply:** Never write code that names two specific languages in a conversion context. Specs only ever see JSON on the wire. If a JSON primitive needs an extension (like `$function_pointer`), it lives in the universal JSON contract, not as a lua-spec-specific or c-spec-specific concept.

**3. Don't propose per-function annotations for type ambiguities (lengths, discriminators, callback signatures).**

**Why:** The user pointed out that "discriminator" is a vocab word the system has no general way to ask about. We can't prompt "which param is the length?" because that pairing convention lives in the function's English documentation, not its types. Asking the user to write annotations means asking them to know specialized vocabulary they didn't sign up for.

**How to apply:** When a function signature has ambiguous types (`char *` with no length, `union` with no tag, `void *` with no signature), expose each parameter as a separate input slot on the box. The user wires the slots according to the function's documentation — `p` from one source, `n` from another. The system never infers pairings; the user expresses them by wiring. If the destination needs a length and no length wire is provided, the wire compile fails with a plain-English fix-it message ("destination needs length, source provides only a pointer — wire a length input here").

**Common thread:** all three rejections are the same principle in different clothes — **SoraMech bends to the language, not the other way around.** Users write idiomatic code in their language. Libraries are used as-is. Specs are self-contained and pair-symmetric. The system stays out of the user's vocabulary.

```

### project_cross_language_wire.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language wire format
description: Dual-ring slot per port (native ring + JSON ring + ordering ring). JSON only at language borders. Per-edge classification at graph load; per-cell precision at runtime.
type: project
originSessionId: 5670858b-274f-49c4-89b8-a4b83ce33d7c
---
Design corrected 2026-05-21 — replaces the older "JSON always" framing.

**Each input slot is a dual-ring buffer.** Per port: one `ring_native` (consumer-language native bytes), one `ring_json` (JSON bytes from cross-language producers), and one `ring_order` of `(which_ring, idx)` tuples in arrival order. Allocate `ring_json` and `ring_order` lazily — same-language-only ports pay nothing for them.

**Push selects ring by per-edge bit.** Producer's spec writes native bytes to `ring_native` if `output_edge_native[j]` is true; otherwise calls `native_to_json` and writes to `ring_json`. Either way, pushes a `(which_ring, idx)` tuple to `ring_order`.

**Pop reads ordering ring first.** Dispatch pops `ring_order`, gets `(which_ring, idx)`, then pops the indicated cell. The consumer's spec receives `(input_data[i], input_native[i])` per input port and dispatches per flag — decode native or decode JSON.

**Why dual-ring instead of per-port classification.** Per-port (slot is all-JSON if any fan-in is cross-lang) is the pessimistic approximation — same-language values eat JSON cost on mixed-fan-in ports. Dual-ring is precise per cell: a port fed by one Lua box and one C box keeps the Lua cells native and JSON-encodes only the C-sourced cells.

**Why JSON for the cross-language ring (not pair-wise paths, not type-annotated raw bytes).** JSON's structure is self-describing — every language has a natural mapping for object/array/number/string/bool/null. Adding language K means K's spec implements its own `native_to_json` and `json_to_native`. N spec-pairs, not N² language-pair paths. The native ring's format is each spec's private choice — Lua may pick msgpack or `cjson.encode` or a custom binary form; C uses `memcpy` of the wrapper struct; Bash uses strings.

**Sentinel primitives for non-JSON-mappable values.** `$ref` (pointer + length into the large-value heap), `$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque` ("these bytes are language-X-internal"). Carried inside the JSON ring as object-shaped sentinels. Cross-language receivers that can't reconstruct fail at wire compile.

**`$function_pointer` reconstruction — wrapper binary + persistent subprocess (issue 318, amended 2026-05-22).** Earlier design had the consumer's spec FFI-cast the raw process-local address. Rejected: FFI is language-pair-specific, biases SoraMech toward the Lua↔C corner, breaks the N-not-N² rule. Replacement: at map-compile time the compiler asks the *producing* spec to compile the referenced function + its enumerable dependencies into a standalone wrapper binary on disk that speaks a small line protocol on stdio. The consumer spec spawns one persistent subprocess per `$function_pointer` it receives and talks to it over the same socket-like channel used for any out-of-process spec. Every language pays the same price; new languages only implement "compile a function to a wrapper binary" — no pair-wise FFI knowledge required.

**Spec `invoke` signature change.** Collapses `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` into one `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags: `int invoke(handle, ..., const int *input_native, int n_inputs, int output_native, void *out_buf, ...)`. The spec dispatches per input internally. This is the contract change that unblocks 306/307's typed marshalling.

**Two compile-time layers stack:**
- **Per-edge classification (issue 312, this design)** — graph loader computes `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` on each box; dispatch routes pushes accordingly. This issue is the wire-format design.
- **Same-language source merge (issue 313, research / blocked)** — concatenate every same-language box's source into one translation unit per language. Boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks; what 313 thins is the spec invocation overhead inside the merged region (direct call into the worker's `lua_State` instead of dlsym + marshal + bridge). The dual-ring slot machinery does NOT collapse — tasks still need slots to wait for sibling inputs. 313 makes the ring cells cheaper to read/write; it doesn't remove them.

**Three rejected design shapes** (kept here so they don't get reinvented):
1. **Handles back-routing to the owning spec** — library functions in the wild can't be modified to use SoraMech-shaped handles. Rejected.
2. **Pair-wise language paths** — every new language would have to grow N-1 translation paths against existing languages. Rejected. The dual-ring's "two rings per slot" is the dimension-cap that prevents this.
3. **Per-function discriminator / length annotations on the wire** — the system has no universal vocabulary to ask "is param 2 the length?" Rejected; the user expresses these by wiring two separate input slots.

**How to apply:** When discussing wire format, slot store shape, dispatch routing, or spec callbacks: think dual-ring (native, JSON, ordering) per slot, per-edge classification at push time, per-cell tag at pop time, JSON-only-at-borders, language-private native bytes everywhere else.

```

### project_custom_translation_specs.md

```markdown
---
name: Custom translation specs per port
description: Users can override the default native/JSON wire path on any input port for any reason — a knob in the wire format vocabulary (issue 246)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Per-port custom translation specs** let the user intervene at a specific input port and replace the default dual-ring decode path with user-written code. The override applies to that one port; the rest of the graph uses the default native-or-JSON path from issue 312.

**Motivating cases (any reason qualifies, not just cross-language):**
- Cross-language ambiguity the default specs can't infer: a C++ class with methods landing at a C box (drop methods? expose as fn pointers? restructure?), a `void *` carrying a libcurl handle, a union whose discriminator is on a separate wire.
- Same-language reshape: massaging a value into a different shape on its way in (rename fields, drop a layer, project a subset) without adding a transform box on the canvas.
- Validation / coercion: clamp a number, enforce a schema, fail loudly on unexpected shapes.

**How it composes with the dual-ring design:**
- The custom spec runs at *pop* time on the consumer side, after the ordering ring has been consulted and the cell has been read from the appropriate ring. The user's code receives the decoded value (native or JSON-decoded) and produces whatever the consumer's `invoke` will see.
- A port with a custom translation gets its own wire color in the editor (issue 245) — visible signal that this port doesn't use the default path.

**Why:** The default native/JSON contract covers the cases JSON's structure handles cleanly. Everything outside that needs a user escape hatch — *and* the same hatch is useful for purely-local "I want this input shaped differently" cases. One mechanism, many uses.

**How to apply:** When the design needs an override knob on the cross-language path, propose "custom translation spec on the destination port" rather than inventing per-function annotations, type discriminator metadata, or producer-side conversion hints (all three were rejected — see feedback_cross_language_pitfalls). The port is the unit of override; the spec is user code; the rest stays default.

```

### project_editor_visual_language.md

```markdown
---
name: Editor visual language for wires
description: Wire color in the canvas editor encodes language pairing across the edge, not just routing kind — a UI invariant future work should respect (issue 245)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Wires are colored by language pairing across the edge**, with a separate color for wires whose destination port carries a user-written custom translation (issue 246). Pre-245 wires were colored purely by routing kind (default slate-blue, comparator branches orange/blue/green).

**The pairing-based palette:**
- **Same-language hop** — the wire carries native bytes; default neutral color.
- **Cross-language hop (forest green, ~`#228b22`)** — different producer/consumer languages; runtime translates via JSON at the wire. The color is a standing reminder that encode + decode is happening on that hop.
- **Custom-translation hop** — a third distinct color signaling the destination port has a user-written translation spec overriding the default path.
- Branch-routing colors (orange/blue/green from comparator boxes) compose on top — routing kind and language pairing are orthogonal axes the editor must show simultaneously.

**Why:** The runtime treats same-lang and cross-lang hops very differently (dual-ring slot design, issue 312), but pre-245 the editor gave the box author no visual signal that the JSON translation step existed. It was invisible until someone read the dispatch code. Translation cost should be legible from the canvas.

**How to apply:** Any future editor work that touches wire rendering must preserve "color encodes language pairing." Don't propose recoloring schemes that overload the cross-language signal onto another concept. New routing concepts get new axes (line style, glyphs, animation) rather than stealing color. When discussing wire visuals, name both axes — routing kind AND language pairing — even if only one is changing.

```

### project_encapsulated_map.md

```markdown
---
name: Encapsulated map as box
description: A sub-map opens as a single box on a parent canvas. Data boxes marked externally-supplied become input ports; write boxes marked externally-consumed become output ports. The documented exception to single-output-per-box (issue 248, amended 2026-05-23)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**A map directory has two ways to be opened:** as the top-level graph (existing map-select UI), or as an **encapsulated box** on the currently-edited parent map (issue 248). Opening through the file browser while a parent map is open instantiates the sub-map as a single box on the parent's canvas.

**The encapsulation contract — symmetric input and output toggles:**
- **Inputs:** any `data` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-supplied" in its inspector. Each such box becomes a typed input port on the encapsulated box.
- **Outputs:** any `write` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-consumed" in its inspector. Each such box surfaces as a **distinct output port** on the encapsulated box. A write box with the toggle on can still write to its `path` if one is set — the file destination and the parent-wire destination are independent.

**Encapsulated maps are the documented exception to issue 218's "single output per box" rule.** They have *N* output ports — one per externally-consumed write box, where *N* may be zero (pure side-effect map), one, or many. Every other box kind still has exactly one output.

**Rejected earlier design (2026-05-21):** packing all write-box outputs into a single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, single wire out. Rejected 2026-05-23 because it would have repurposed file-writing machinery to emit strings into wires — substituting one mechanism for another. The symmetric toggle design preserves the `write` box's "terminate a value" semantics and treats the destination kind as a mode toggle.

**Why:** Encapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph. The parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals — it sees declared input ports, declared output ports, and known semantics. Sub-maps can be edited independently, reused across parents, and packaged once for distribution. This is the closest SoraMech gets to "user-defined functions" while staying graph-native.

**How to apply:** When discussing map composition, reuse, or "how do users build libraries of behavior" — encapsulation is the answer. Don't propose alternative function-abstraction mechanisms (named subgraphs as text references, macro-style inlining, blob-packed outputs) without explicitly weighing them against the symmetric-toggle shape. Both toggles (`externally-supplied` on data boxes, `externally-consumed` on write boxes) are the user-facing port-declaration mechanism — don't invent a separate "ports manifest" file.

```

### project_soramech.md

```markdown
---
name: SoraMech project context
description: Core architecture decisions, file layout, and execution model for SoraMech, across phase 2 (current) and phase 3 (designed)
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
SoraMech is a visual FSM/dataflow editor and execution engine at /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/.

**Why:** Primary use case is LLM orchestration on the SoraMind Alpine cluster. Strings flow between boxes like variables. History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.

**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**
- `src/006-server-main.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy. No runner management.
- Runner — phase 2: `src/007-runner-main.lua` (synchronous Lua). Phase 3: `soramech-pool` (C binary, designed in issues 301–311, not yet built).
- `assets/index.html` — vanilla JS canvas editor. Editor only — no run button. Compile button (issue 222) is a phase 2 placeholder; it triggers the phase 3 build pipeline (issue 219).

**Key architecture decisions (current truth):**
- Each box is its own JSON file in `boxes/<id>.json`. Connections written to BOTH endpoint files; loader validates both ends agree — hard error if not.
- **Single output wire per box** (issue 218 complete). No `outputs` array. The function returns one value; routing is by `from_branch` on the connection.
- **Comparator-based branching** (issue 210) — replaces the earlier `branch` box kind with named ports. A box may carry a `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires `lt`/`eq`/`gt` connections. No spec is invoked for comparators.
- **Iterator boxes** (issue 221) — pure routing primitives, no `ref`/`fn`. Dispatch layer cycles through `iterator_outputs` based on a per-task counter.
- **Phase 2 drivers** are shell scripts under `drivers/` (one process per call, stdout as channel). **Phase 3 language specs** are `.so` libraries under `langs/<name>/spec.so` loaded via `dlopen` (issue 303). Lua and C are in-process; Bash is out-of-process via Unix domain socket.
- Data files: per-map JSON in `data/`. Section-level `constant` flag. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.
- State/ephemeral: `tmp/` is a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Phase 2 writes `last-run.json` (single doc). Phase 3 writes `last-run.jsonl` (JSON Lines, issue 311) — decoupled from the editor, consumed by LLMs / CLI viewers / test harness.
- **Phase 3 runtime model**: C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool; per-task slots in process heap (issue 302) with refcounting and a separate large-value heap; dispatch layer (304) is the worker action; graph loader is C (305), no embedded Lua at the runner level. Phase 2's synchronous executor retires when phase 3 lands.

**How to apply:** When working on any component, respect the three-way separation. Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server. Map directory format is the only shared contract. The phase 2 driver model and the phase 3 spec model coexist conceptually (phase 2 is current, phase 3 is fully designed) but the runtime mechanism differs entirely; box JSON and the editor are unchanged across the cutover.

```

### project_threading.md

```markdown
---
name: threading_model
description: SoraMech's threading model — phase 2 synchronous, phase 3 SoraMech-owned C thread pool with per-port slots and language specs
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
**Phase 2 (current)**: synchronous executor in `src/004-executor.lua`. Single-threaded, sequential box execution. One driver shell-out per box call. The phase 2 path goes away when phase 3 lands — no fallback, no coroutine intermediate.

**Phase 3 (designed, not yet built)**: C pool runner with a SoraMech-owned thread pool. The 3d-rts pool at `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` is the **design reference**, not vendored — SoraMech owns its pool implementation so the spawn primitive, worker context, init barrier, and iterator-pinning extensions are all under our control. The architecture is fully specified across issues 301–313.

Key phase 3 concepts:
- **Per-input-port slots** (not per-task), allocated at graph load and durable for the run. Each slot is a ring buffer (`n_cells` cells of `cell_capacity` bytes). 1-cell slots use peek-not-drain (literals, single-push wires); N-cell slots use pop-and-drain (queued / multi-push wires). No per-slot refcounting — slot lifetime is the whole run.
- **Tasks are ephemeral**: spawned dynamically by the dispatch layer when a box's input set is ready. Tasks carry just `box_id` and a counter snapshot. Box state (counter, input slots, language handle) is durable.
- **Language specs** under `langs/<name>/spec.so`, loaded via `dlopen` at startup. Uniform `lang_spec_t`. No language is privileged.
- **Same-language fast path** (issue 312): wire format defaults to JSON, but two adjacent same-language boxes use the language's native serialization (Lua `lua_dump`, C struct memcpy). Compile-time wire classification picks the path.
- **In-process specs** (Lua, C) via `lua_pcall` / `dlsym`. **Out-of-process specs** (Bash) via Unix domain sockets to a persistent per-worker subprocess.
- **Dispatch layer** (304) is the worker-side action: pop inputs → branch on box mode → invoke spec → push to downstream input slots → end. No blocking, no wait lists; tasks spawn on input arrival and run to completion.
- **Iterator and comparator routing** in the dispatch layer. Comparator runs the function and routes by output value. Iterator skips the function and routes by per-box counter (atomic spawn-time increment). Iterator tasks parallelize across workers; ordering preserved via per-push counter tags on consumer slots.
- **No-null rule** (issue 230): every input port must be wired, given a literal, or marked optional. Compile fails on missing inputs.
- **Init barrier**: pool startup waits until every worker has run every spec's `init(worker_idx)` before submitting tasks. Avoids tasks landing on uninitialized handles.
- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program.
- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations tie up a worker. Pool size is the budget. Cooperative split (kickoff + check-done iterator) avoids holding a worker. See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.

**Effil is explicitly NOT used.** Coroutines are not used. The C pool is the chosen mechanism. 3d-rts is referenced as design inspiration, not vendored.

**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC: phase 2 is synchronous shell-out drivers; phase 3 is the SoraMech-owned C pool runner with `lang_spec_t`, per-port slot stores, and dispatch-layer routing. Never suggest effil. 3d-rts is a reference, not a dependency. Issues 301–313 carry the design.

```

Automated behaviors (\"from now on when X\", \"each time X\", \"whenever X\", \"before/after X\") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions (\"allow X\", \"add permission\", \"move permission to\"), env vars (\"set X=Y\"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: \"allow npm commands\", \"add bq permission to global settings\", \"move permission to user settings\", \"set DEBUG=true\", \"when claude stops show X\". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.\n- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: \"rebind ctrl+s\", \"add a chord shortcut\", \"change the submit key\", \"customize keybindings\".\n- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.\n- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.\n- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. \"check the deploy every 5 minutes\", \"keep running /babysit-prs\"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.\n- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run (\"run this once at 3pm\", \"remind me to check X tomorrow\").\n- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).\nTRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.\nSKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.\n- frontend-design:frontend-design: Create distinctive, production-grade frontend interfaces with high design quality. Update every connection that referenced a renamed slot:\n   - `to_input` in the connection record on this box\n   - The corresponding side on the source box (connections are stored in both\n     endpoint files; both must be updated atomically).\n4. Keep at least one slot for the variadic input (never shrink below `text_0`).\n\nMiddle-port removal is handled by the same rename-and-compact step: remove the cut\nslot, shift all higher-indexed slots down, update their wires. The user always sees\na dense, gap-free list of ports.\n\n## Open questions before implementing Part B\n- Rename atomicity: the server's `PUT /maps/:name/boxes/:id` writes one box at a\n  time. Updating the connection in the source box requires a second PUT. These are\n  two separate writes — consider whether a partial failure leaves the map in an\n  inconsistent state, and whether a `PUT /maps/:name/connections` batch endpoint\n  is worth adding first.\n- Should the file browser parser set `variadic_inputs` automatically when it\n  detects `...` in a Lua signature, and if so, which argument specifically?\n\n  -- nah let's just make the user set the variadic property manually. Unless we can put it in the language driver\n     somehow? but I don't think that's really possible in the design. Thoughts?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Part A: implement `libs/text.lua` with `M.concat(sep, ...)`.\n2. Part B schema: add `variadic_inputs` to box schema and validator.\n3. Part B editor: auto-grow on wire connect; auto-shrink + rename on wire disconnect.\n4. Part B inspector: variadic toggle per input port.\n5. Part B parser: auto-detect `...` in Lua and set `variadic_inputs`.\n\n## Future development ideas\n\n### Language-spec-driven variadic detection\n\nCurrently the editor uses hard-coded heuristics per language to find\nvariadic indicators in a function signature (Lua: literal `...`, Bash:\n`$@` after `shift`). The cleaner architecture mirrors the phase 3\nlanguage-spec model (issue 303): each language declares its own way\nto recognize and surface variadic parameters, and the file-browser\nparser asks the language spec rather than embedding the rules.\n\nConcretely, the editor side of a language spec\n(`langs/<name>/lexer.js` or a sibling `parser.js`) could expose:\n\n```js\n// Returns { name, inputs: [\"sep\", \"text\"], variadic_inputs: [\"text\"] }\n// for `function M.concat(sep, ...)` in Lua, or\n// `concat() { local sep=\"$1\"; shift; ... \"$@\" }` in Bash.\nfunction parse_function_signature(source, fn_name) { ... }\n```\n\nThe editor still calls the same on-select handler; the language spec\nis responsible for deciding how to translate native variadic syntax\ninto the editor's `(inputs, variadic_inputs)` model.\n\n### Variadic shapes that don't map cleanly to an array\n\nThe current model assumes variadic = an ordered series of positional\nslots. That fits Lua `...`, C `va_list`, Bash `\"$@\"`, JavaScript rest\nparams, etc. It does not fit:\n\n- **Keyword arguments** (Python `**kwargs`, Ruby keyword splats) —\n  these are key/value pairs, not positional. A box would need\n  named-slot pairs the user labels per slot, not auto-numbered\n  `_0` / `_1` / `_2`.\n- **Tagged unions / discriminated lists** (Rust enum lists, Haskell\n  variadic via heterogeneous lists) — each entry has a type tag in\n  addition to a value. Two-field slots, or per-slot type metadata.\n- **Streaming inputs** (generators, channels, iterators) — the\n  consumer doesn't know in advance how many values arrive. This is\n  closer to issue 213's queued-input model than to variadic.\n\nA future revision of the editor's variadic UI could let language\nspecs choose between several \"variadic shapes\":\n\n| shape           | slot model                          | example use      |\n|-----------------|-------------------------------------|------------------|\n| `positional`    | `<base>_<index>` ordered (current)  | Lua `...`        |\n| `keyed`         | per-slot `(key, value)` pairs       | Python `**kwargs`|\n| `tagged`        | per-slot `(tag, value)` pairs       | discriminated unions |\n| `stream`        | one slot, queued (issue 213)        | iterators        |\n\nEach shape would have its own auto-grow rule and inspector controls.\nThe language spec declares which shape applies to a given variadic\nparameter, and the editor renders accordingly.\n\nThis is speculative — the positional shape covers every shipped\nlanguage so far. Capturing it here so the design door stays open.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `libs/ollama.lua` — reference pattern for a library box\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — wire connect/disconnect events\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — input port list, toggle rendering\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator (`variadic_inputs` field)\n- `src/005-http-server.lua` — PUT box endpoint (rename propagation)\n- `issues/208-port-literal-values.md` — `sep` will likely use literal port values\n",

A user skimming the map sees the\nstructure but not the content.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nIf a port has a literal value set in the inspector, **the canvas\nlabel for that port shows the value instead of the port's name**.\nThe inspector still shows the original port name in its name field\n(unchanged) and the value in its value field (unchanged) — only the\ncanvas rendering changes.\n\nExamples:\n\n| port name | literal value     | canvas label |\n|-----------|-------------------|--------------|\n| `sep`     | `\"\\n\\n\"`          | `\"\\n\\n\"`     |\n| `prompt`  | (none)            | `prompt`     |\n| `path`    | `\"./input.txt\"`   | `\"./input.txt\"` |\n| `count`   | `5`               | `5`          |\n\nThe value is the same string the user typed; quotes are part of\nhow the user wrote it. Long values get truncated with an ellipsis\nat a reasonable width (~24 chars?) and the full value shows in a\ntooltip on hover.\n\n### Why\n\nThis is the same idea as a spreadsheet cell showing the rendered\nvalue while the formula bar shows the formula. A user wants to see\n*what the program does* — the configured value — without having to\ninspect each box one at a time. The port name is meta-information\n(useful when wiring, useful in the inspector); the value is the\ninformation (useful when reading the map).\n\n### Wires override values\n\nIf a wire is connected to a port, the wire is the source of truth\nand any literal value is ignored at runtime. The canvas label in\nthat case shows the **port name**, not the value — the value isn't\nwhat's flowing through, and showing it would mislead.           "content":"# 236 — Box header shows filename; output label shows `fn_name()` call form\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA call box's header (the bold text at the top of the box on the\ncanvas) currently displays the box's label — by default, the\nfunction name (e.g. `concat`, `read_text`, `prompt_ollama`). The\noutput port on the right edge has a generic label (`output` /\n`result` / whatever the parser produced).\n\nFor a user reading a map, the header gives one of the two pieces\nof relevant identity (the function), but the other piece — *which\nfile the function comes from* — is missing from the visible box.\nYou can see `concat` and not know whether it is `libs/text.lua`'s\nconcat or some other module's concat without opening the inspector\nand reading `ref`.\n\nThe single output label, `output`, is generic and conveys nothing\nabout what's being computed.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nReinterpret the two text slots on a box:\n\n- **Box header (top)** = the **filename** of `ref` (basename, no\n  path prefix, e.g. `text.lua`). This is the module / file the\n  function lives in.\n- **Output port label (right edge)** = the function call form,\n  `fn_name()`, e.g. `concat()`, `read_text()`, `prompt_ollama()`.\n  This reads as \"this wire carries the return value of calling\n  fn_name.\"\n\nSo a box that calls `concat` from `libs/text.lua` reads, top to\nbottom on the canvas:\n\n```\n┌─ text.lua ────────────────┐\n│ ● sep      \"\\n\\n\"          │\n│ ● text_0                   │   concat() ●\n│ ● text_1                   │\n└────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\n(Combined with issue 235, the `sep` literal also shows on the\ncanvas — included here for illustration of how the canvas reads as\na whole.)\n\n### Why this split\n\nA reader scanning a map mentally parses it as a series of function\ncalls. The function call form `fn_name()` is the natural way to\nread \"this is the value of calling fn_name with these inputs.\" The\nfilename header sits one layer up: \"this function comes from this\nmodule.\" Together they read like an annotated call site — module\non top, return value on the side.\n\nIt also frees the box header from having to be unique. Right now\nthe default label is the function name, which collides across\nboxes that all call the same function. The filename groups by\nmodule — many boxes can share `text.lua` as their header and that\nis fine; what distinguishes them is what they compute and how\nthey are wired.\n\n### Label override\n\nThe user-editable `box.label` field remains. If a user sets an\nexplicit label, it overrides the filename in the header. Use case:\nmultiple boxes in the same map call `text.concat`, and the user\nwants to name them by their role (\"join paragraphs\", \"join CSV\nrow\") rather than by module. The override is intentional and only\napplied when set; default behavior is filename-from-ref.\n\nThe output port label is not user-editable in this issue — it is\nalways derived from `fn`. (If a use case appears, add it later.)\n\n### Filename derivation\n\n`ref` is a path like `libs/text.lua` or `maps/foo/src/echo.sh`.\nTake the basename (`text.lua`, `echo.sh`). Do not strip the\nextension — the extension says which language driver runs, which\nis information the user cares about.\n\nFor boxes without a `ref` (branch boxes, comparators, future\ndispatch-layer primitives like the data source from issue 229),\nfall back to the kind name (`branch`, `data`, etc.) in the header\nslot, and skip the `fn()` output label (or show the primitive's\nown conventional output name).\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `assets/js/002-boxes.js::draw_box` — header text path:\n   - If `box.label` is set and non-empty, use it (current behavior).\n   - Else, derive from `box.ref`: basename of the path string.\n   - Else (no ref), use `box.kind` as a final fallback.\n2. Output port label path: when `box.fn` is set, render\n   `${box.fn}()` instead of `output` / `result`. Otherwise leave\n   the existing default.\n3. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — the inspector's \"label\" field\n   shows the override value (the explicit user-set label) and its\n   placeholder shows what the canvas is using by default. So the\n   user sees \"currently displayed: text.lua (from ref)\" and can\n   override.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Path vs basename for the header**: a deeply-nested ref like\n  `maps/foo/src/sub/echo.sh` becomes just `echo.sh` in the header.\n  Is the parent dir worth keeping (`sub/echo.sh`) for disambiguation?\n  Probably not by default — the inspector shows the full ref —\n  but worth revisiting if collisions cause confusion.\n- **Branch / data / future primitives**: their headers and output\n  labels need conventions of their own. Capture per-kind defaults\n  in one place (a small kind-to-header map) so future kinds add\n  one entry.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box draw routine\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — label field + placeholder hint\n- `issues/completed/207-source-file-browser-and-port-auto-population.md`\n  — ref/fn pairing established here\n- `issues/completed/210-llm-route-box.md` — single-output redesign\n  this issue's `fn()` label leans on\n- `issues/235-literal-value-replaces-port-name-on-canvas.md` — sister\n  display change for input ports\n",

The\nfile browser (issue 211, 211a) sees the map's own `src/` directory\nplus the unified pipeline dirs the runner sets up, but the set of\n\"bundled / default\" library locations the editor offers is\nhard-coded in the server / file-browser logic.\n\nIf a user wants to drop in their own personal library of bundled\nscripts (e.g. their own `text-extras.lua`, their own\n`my-team-helpers/` directory) and have the editor's file browser\ntreat them as first-class default refs, there is no per-deployment\nway to point the server at additional directories. The user can override any subset by editing the\nfile.\n\n### File location and format\n\nPath: `config/editor-server.lua` (returns a Lua table) or\n`config/editor-server.json`. Lean toward the Lua table — every\nother config in this project is Lua, and a Lua return-table lets\nthe user compute paths if needed (e.g. `os.getenv(\"HOME\") .. \"/my-libs\"`).\n\nShape:\n\n```lua\nreturn {\n  port = 7474,\n  map_root = \"maps\",\n  asset_dir = \"assets\",\n  bundled_script_dirs = {\n    \"libs\",           -- the in-tree default\n    -- \"~/.soramech/my-libs\",  -- example user override\n  },\n  tmp_dir = \"tmp\",\n}\n```\n\nA startup helper in `src/006-server-main.lua` loads the config,\nfills in defaults, and passes the resolved table down to the HTTP\nserver module. The server prints the resolved config on boot so\nthe user can confirm what's in effect.\n\n### File browser surfacing\n\nThe file browser (issue 211 + 211a) currently lists the map's own\n`src/` and the pipeline-resolved bundled dirs.     "content":"# 234 — Middle-click duplicates the selected box (with wires)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA box on the canvas can be selected (single click) and edited via\nthe inspector, but there is no shortcut for \"make me another one\njust like this.\" A user who wants to repeat a configured box has\nto:\n\n1. Right-click → \"add box here\" to spawn a fresh empty box.\n2. Reopen the file browser, re-pick the same ref / fn.\n3. Re-type all the literal input values.\n4. Re-wire every upstream connection by hand.\n\nFor a box with several literal values and several incoming wires\nthis is many clicks of pure repetition, and any one of them is a\nchance to typo a value or miss a wire.\n\nMiddle-mouse currently has no editor behavior other than the\nbrowser's default scroll-anchor (which is itself disruptive on a\ncanvas app).\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n**When a box is selected and the user does a short middle-mouse\nclick (not a drag) anywhere on the canvas**, the editor creates a\nduplicate of the selected box at the cursor position. The duplicate\ncarries over:\n\n- `ref`, `fn`, `kind`, `outputs`, `variadic_inputs` — same function\n  bound to the new box.\n- Every input port, including its literal value (if any).\n- Every wire whose destination is the original box: a matching wire\n  is created from the same source box / output to the new box's\n  same-named input. Outgoing wires (where the original is the\n  source) are NOT duplicated — multiple boxes fanning out from one\n  source is the normal case; multiple boxes converging on the same\n  downstream port is not.\n\nThe duplicate gets a fresh `id` and a `ui.x / ui.y` at the cursor\nlocation. The label is the original's label suffixed `(copy)` (or\n`(copy 2)`, `(copy 3)` if the suffix is already present) — same\nnaming pattern most desktop UIs use.\n\nA middle-drag (the cursor moved more than a few pixels between\npress and release) is not a duplicate. Reserve that gesture for\nfuture pan / other use; for now it is a no-op rather than an\naccidental copy.\n\nIf no box is selected, middle-click is a no-op (with maybe a\ntoast / status hint, \"select a box to duplicate it\").\n\n### Why middle-click\n\nRight-click already opens the context menu (issue 212). Left-click\nselects / deselects. Middle-click is the only unused primary\nbutton, and the \"click on empty canvas to place\" muscle memory from\nadd-box mode transfers cleanly: select source → middle-click target.\n\n### Why duplicate incoming wires by default\n\nThe whole reason to duplicate is \"I want another node fed by the\nsame data.\" Forcing the user to re-wire defeats the gesture.\nOutgoing wires are skipped because the user usually wants the copy\nto feed something *new* downstream — that's the half they're about\nto wire up.\n\n### Open question — duplicate-with-no-wires variant?\n\nHold a modifier (`Shift+middle-click`?) to duplicate without\nwires? Defer until someone asks; the wireless version is just \"add\na fresh box and browse to the same fn,\" which the right-click menu\nalready covers.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `assets/js/005-app.js` — middle-mouse handlers:\n   - `mousedown` (button 1): record press position + selected box id.\n   - `mouseup` (button 1): if movement ≤ threshold and a box is\n     selected, call `duplicate_box(selected_id, cursor_world_pos)`.\n   - `preventDefault` on the mousedown to suppress browser\n     scroll-anchor behavior.\n2. New module function `Boxes.duplicate(src_box, x, y)`:\n   - Clone the box JSON, assign a new id, set `ui.x/ui.y`.\n   - Suffix the label with `(copy)` / `(copy N)`.\n   - POST to the server (existing create-box endpoint).\n3. Wire duplication: iterate every connection in the map whose\n   `to_box == src_box.id`. For each, POST a matching connection\n   with `to_box = new_box.id` (same `to_input`, same\n   `from_box` / `from_output`).\n4. Update local Boxes cache and re-render. Select the new box so\n   the user can immediately edit / nudge it.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/005-app.js` — pointer event handlers, current\n  right-click context menu lives here.\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — local box cache + create flow.\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — `create_connection`, wire data model.\n- `src/005-http-server.lua` — existing POST endpoints for boxes\n  and connections.\n- `issues/completed/212-editor-interaction-modes.md` — established\n  the right-click and tool-mode patterns this issue extends.\n",
    "structuredPatch":[],

    "content":"# 235 — Literal value replaces port name on the canvas (when set)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nEach input port renders as a dot on the left edge of a box, with\nthe port's name (e.g. `text`, `sep`, `prompt`) drawn next to it on\nthe canvas. The literal value of that port — when one has been\ntyped into the inspector (issue 208 / 224) — does not appear on the\ncanvas at all. To see what value is bound, the user opens the\ninspector and reads the value field.\n\nFor a box like `concat(sep, text_0, text_1)` where `sep` is a\nliteral `\"\\n\\n\"`, the canvas shows the parameter name `sep` but\nnot the actual separator. A user skimming the map sees the\nstructure but not the content.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nIf a port has a literal value set in the inspector, **the canvas\nlabel for that port shows the value instead of the port's name**.\nThe inspector still shows the original port name in its name field\n(unchanged) and the value in its value field (unchanged) — only the\ncanvas rendering changes.\n\nExamples:\n\n| port name | literal value     | canvas label |\n|-----------|-------------------|--------------|\n| `sep`     | `\"\\n\\n\"`          | `\"\\n\\n\"`     |\n| `prompt`  | (none)            | `prompt`     |\n| `path`    | `\"./input.txt\"`   | `\"./input.txt\"` |\n| `count`   | `5`               | `5`          |\n\nThe value is the same string the user typed; quotes are part of\nhow the user wrote it. Long values get truncated with an ellipsis\nat a reasonable width (~24 chars?) and the full value shows in a\ntooltip on hover.\n\n### Why\n\nThis is the same idea as a spreadsheet cell showing the rendered\nvalue while the formula bar shows the formula. A user wants to see\n*what the program does* — the configured value — without having to\ninspect each box one at a time. The port name is meta-information\n(useful when wiring, useful in the inspector); the value is the\ninformation (useful when reading the map).\n\n### Wires override values\n\nIf a wire is connected to a port, the wire is the source of truth\nand any literal value is ignored at runtime. The canvas label in\nthat case shows the **port name**, not the value — the value isn't\nwhat's flowing through, and showing it would mislead. Three states:\n\n- No wire, no value → show port name.\n- No wire, literal value set → show the value.\n- Wire connected → show the port name (value, if any, is dormant).\n\n### Edge cases\n\n- **Multi-line value** (e.g. a prompt with `\\n` in it): render the\n  first line only on the canvas, ellipsis if there's more, full\n  value in the tooltip.\n- **Empty string value** (`\"\"`): treat as \"no value\" — show the\n  port name. Otherwise the user types accidentally and the port\n  silently disappears from view.\n- **Variadic slots** (`text_0`, `text_1`, …): the same rule\n  applies per slot. A variadic group with each slot's value shown\n  is one of the strongest cases for this feature.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `assets/js/002-boxes.js::draw_box` — the loop that draws\n   input port labels. Replace the unconditional `port.name` with:\n   ```\n   const wire_attached = wire_targets_port(box, port);\n   const has_value = port.value != null && port.value !== \"\";\n   const label = (!wire_attached && has_value) ? truncate(port.value) : port.name;\n   ```\n2. Hover / tooltip: if the canvas label is a truncated value,\n   register a small hit-region so the existing tooltip mechanism\n   (or a fresh one) can show the full value on mouseover.\n3. Re-render on inspector value edit: the existing autosave path\n   already invalidates the canvas; verify it still triggers a\n   redraw after this change.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — port label rendering\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — value field that drives the data\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — `wire_targets_port` helper (or write\n  one if not present)\n- `issues/completed/208-port-literal-values.md` — established\n  literal values; this issue surfaces them visually\n- `issues/completed/224-editable-port-names-and-canvas-value-edit.md`\n  — explicitly deferred canvas-value-edit; this is a related but\n  smaller display-only change, not the editing UI from 224\n",
    "structuredPatch":[],

    "content":"# 236 — Box header shows filename; output label shows `fn_name()` call form\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA call box's header (the bold text at the top of the box on the\ncanvas) currently displays the box's label — by default, the\nfunction name (e.g. `concat`, `read_text`, `prompt_ollama`). The\noutput port on the right edge has a generic label (`output` /\n`result` / whatever the parser produced).\n\nFor a user reading a map, the header gives one of the two pieces\nof relevant identity (the function), but the other piece — *which\nfile the function comes from* — is missing from the visible box.\nYou can see `concat` and not know whether it is `libs/text.lua`'s\nconcat or some other module's concat without opening the inspector\nand reading `ref`.\n\nThe single output label, `output`, is generic and conveys nothing\nabout what's being computed.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nReinterpret the two text slots on a box:\n\n- **Box header (top)** = the **filename** of `ref` (basename, no\n  path prefix, e.g. `text.lua`). This is the module / file the\n  function lives in.\n- **Output port label (right edge)** = the function call form,\n  `fn_name()`, e.g. `concat()`, `read_text()`, `prompt_ollama()`.\n  This reads as \"this wire carries the return value of calling\n  fn_name.\"\n\nSo a box that calls `concat` from `libs/text.lua` reads, top to\nbottom on the canvas:\n\n```\n┌─ text.lua ────────────────┐\n│ ● sep      \"\\n\\n\"          │\n│ ● text_0                   │   concat() ●\n│ ● text_1                   │\n└────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\n(Combined with issue 235, the `sep` literal also shows on the\ncanvas — included here for illustration of how the canvas reads as\na whole.)\n\n### Why this split\n\nA reader scanning a map mentally parses it as a series of function\ncalls. The function call form `fn_name()` is the natural way to\nread \"this is the value of calling fn_name with these inputs.\" The\nfilename header sits one layer up: \"this function comes from this\nmodule.\" Together they read like an annotated call site — module\non top, return value on the side.\n\nIt also frees the box header from having to be unique. Right now\nthe default label is the function name, which collides across\nboxes that all call the same function. The filename groups by\nmodule — many boxes can share `text.lua` as their header and that\nis fine; what distinguishes them is what they compute and how\nthey are wired.\n\n### Label override\n\nThe user-editable `box.label` field remains. If a user sets an\nexplicit label, it overrides the filename in the header. Use case:\nmultiple boxes in the same map call `text.concat`, and the user\nwants to name them by their role (\"join paragraphs\", \"join CSV\nrow\") rather than by module. The override is intentional and only\napplied when set; default behavior is filename-from-ref.\n\nThe output port label is not user-editable in this issue — it is\nalways derived from `fn`. (If a use case appears, add it later.)\n\n### Filename derivation\n\n`ref` is a path like `libs/text.lua` or `maps/foo/src/echo.sh`.\nTake the basename (`text.lua`, `echo.sh`). Do not strip the\nextension — the extension says which language driver runs, which\nis information the user cares about.\n\nFor boxes without a `ref` (branch boxes, comparators, future\ndispatch-layer primitives like the data source from issue 229),\nfall back to the kind name (`branch`, `data`, etc.) in the header\nslot, and skip the `fn()` output label (or show the primitive's\nown conventional output name).\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `assets/js/002-boxes.js::draw_box` — header text path:\n   - If `box.label` is set and non-empty, use it (current behavior).\n   - Else, derive from `box.ref`: basename of the path string.\n   - Else (no ref), use `box.kind` as a final fallback.\n2. Output port label path: when `box.fn` is set, render\n   `${box.fn}()` instead of `output` / `result`. Otherwise leave\n   the existing default.\n3. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — the inspector's \"label\" field\n   shows the override value (the explicit user-set label) and its\n   placeholder shows what the canvas is using by default. So the\n   user sees \"currently displayed: text.lua (from ref)\" and can\n   override.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Path vs basename for the header**: a deeply-nested ref like\n  `maps/foo/src/sub/echo.sh` becomes just `echo.sh` in the header.\n  Is the parent dir worth keeping (`sub/echo.sh`) for disambiguation?\n  Probably not by default — the inspector shows the full ref —\n  but worth revisiting if collisions cause confusion.\n- **Branch / data / future primitives**: their headers and output\n  labels need conventions of their own. Capture per-kind defaults\n  in one place (a small kind-to-header map) so future kinds add\n  one entry.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box draw routine\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — label field + placeholder hint\n- `issues/completed/207-source-file-browser-and-port-auto-population.md`\n  — ref/fn pairing established here\n- `issues/completed/210-llm-route-box.md` — single-output redesign\n  this issue's `fn()` label leans on\n- `issues/235-literal-value-replaces-port-name-on-canvas.md` — sister\n  display change for input ports\n",
    "structuredPatch":[],
    "type":"create",

    "content":"# 237 — Expand the bundled string-manipulation library\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`libs/text.lua` (created in issue 217) exposes two functions:\n\n- `M.concat(sep, ...)` — variadic join with a separator\n- `M.split(text, sep)` — split a string on a plain separator,\n  returns a JSON-encoded array\n\nThat covers two of the most common string operations and was\ndeliberately minimal — just enough for the demo map that drove 217.\nA user wanting to upper-case, lower-case, find-and-replace, trim,\nor substring has to either write the function themselves into a\nproject-local file, or fall back to a Lua call box pointing at\n`string.upper` / `string.gsub` directly (which works but is more\ntyping per box).\n\nThere is also no canonical home for \"the string library that ships\nwith the editor.\" `libs/text.lua` exists but its scope was set by\none issue's needs, not by a broader plan.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n`libs/text.lua` grows into a small, opinionated standard library\nof string operations, each wired to be variadic-friendly and\nsingle-output where it makes sense. The full set in this issue:\n\n| function                          | inputs                          | output                          |\n|-----------------------------------|----------------------------------|---------------------------------|\n| `M.concat(sep, ...)`              | sep, variadic text               | joined string (already exists)  |\n| `M.split(text, sep)`              | text, sep                        | JSON array of parts (exists)    |\n| `M.upper(text)`                   | text                             | upper-cased string              |\n| `M.lower(text)`                   | text                             | lower-cased string              |\n| `M.trim(text)`                    | text                             | leading + trailing ws stripped  |\n| `M.replace(text, find, repl)`     | text, find, repl                 | every occurrence replaced       |\n| `M.replace_first(text, find, repl)`| text, find, repl                | first occurrence only           |\n| `M.contains(text, needle)`        | text, needle                     | boolean (as `\"true\"`/`\"false\"`) |\n| `M.starts_with(text, prefix)`     | text, prefix                     | boolean                         |\n| `M.ends_with(text, suffix)`       | text, suffix                     | boolean                         |\n| `M.length(text)`                  | text                             | integer (as string on wire)     |\n| `M.substring(text, start, len)`   | text, start, len (1-indexed)     | substring                       |\n\nAll `find` / `prefix` / `suffix` arguments are **plain strings**,\nnot Lua patterns — same convention as `M.split`. A user who wants\npatterns can call `string.gsub` directly via a call box. The\nlibrary's job is \"common case, no surprises.\"\n\n`M.replace_first` is a separate function rather than a flag on\n`replace` because the editor has no boolean-port primitive yet\n(literal values are strings; \"all or first\" toggles cleanly\nbetween two function names). Could collapse later when a primitive\nboolean exists.\n\n### Companion info.md\n\nUpdate `libs/text.lua.info.md` so each function gets its own entry\nwith inputs / outputs / one-line description. Issue 207's file\nbrowser parses signatures from source; the info.md is the\nhuman-skim version. (Per CLAUDE.md: prefer reading info.md over\nsource for an overview.)\n\n### Why these specifically\n\nSkim a handful of maps and the same operations show up: cleaning\ninput (trim), normalizing case (upper / lower), simple\nsubstitution (replace), boolean guards (contains / starts_with /\nends_with), array slicing (substring). The list above covers the\n\"would you have written this as a helper anyway?\" cases without\nsprawling into a kitchen-sink std lib.\n\nOperations explicitly **not** in this issue:\n\n- Regex / pattern matching — a separate `libs/regex.lua` issue.\n  Pattern syntax is its own UI problem (which dialect? escape\n  rules?) and deserves a dedicated home.\n- Encode / decode (base64, URL, hex) — separate `libs/codec.lua`.\n- Format strings (`printf`-style) — single-output-wire constraint\n  makes the call shape awkward; revisit when the language spec for\n  format string handling firms up.\n\n### Bundled location convention\n\nFiles in `libs/` are the bundled, edit-as-default modules every\nmap can `ref` directly without per-map setup. This issue does not\nchange that — it just fills out one of those bundled modules.\n\nA future per-language convention (issue 303 territory) might split\n`libs/` by language (`libs/lua/text.lua`, `libs/c/text.c`,\n`libs/bash/text.sh`). Today everything in `libs/` is Lua; revisit\nthe split when a second language ships a bundled standard library.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `libs/text.lua` — append the new functions. Each is a 1-3 line\n   wrapper over a `string.*` builtin or a small primitive. Keep\n   them order-aligned with the table above for readability.\n2. `libs/text.lua.info.md` — add one entry per new function\n   following the existing format. Include the \"plain string, not\n   pattern\" note where applicable.\n3. A small test map (`tests/maps/text-lib/`?) — one box per\n   function, hand-traced expected outputs. The phase-2 integration\n   tests can pick it up automatically (issue 311 wiring).\n4. The demo for the current phase should pick up at least one or\n   two of these on its display path so the user sees the library\n   in action.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `libs/text.lua` — host of the new functions\n- `libs/text.lua.info.md` — documentation companion\n- `issues/completed/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — founded\n  this library with concat + split\n- `issues/238-editor-http-server-config-file.md` — paired issue\n  that makes \"where do bundled libs live\" configurable, so a user\n  can add their own bundled-default directory alongside `libs/`\n",
    "structuredPatch":[],
    "type":"create",
    "userModified":false,

    "content":"# 238 — Editor HTTP server config file (default bundled-script locations)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe editor's HTTP server (`src/005-http-server.lua`, issue 105) is\nlaunched with map-relative paths discovered at startup time. The\nfile browser (issue 211, 211a) sees the map's own `src/` directory\nplus the unified pipeline dirs the runner sets up, but the set of\n\"bundled / default\" library locations the editor offers is\nhard-coded in the server / file-browser logic.\n\nIf a user wants to drop in their own personal library of bundled\nscripts (e.g. their own `text-extras.lua`, their own\n`my-team-helpers/` directory) and have the editor's file browser\ntreat them as first-class default refs, there is no per-deployment\nway to point the server at additional directories. They would have\nto edit the server source.\n\nThere is also no record of the editor's runtime configuration —\nports, default map dir, asset dir, the bundled lib dirs — in a\nconfig file the user can read or version. The defaults live in\ncode.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nIntroduce a config file the editor's HTTP server reads at startup\nto learn:\n\n- **Server port** (default `7474` or whichever current default).\n- **Map root directory** (default `maps/`).\n- **Bundled script locations** — a list of directory paths the\n  file browser exposes as default-available refs, distinct from\n  the current map's own `src/`. Default list includes `libs/`.\n- **Asset directory** for the editor (default `assets/`).\n- **Log / tmp directory** if relevant (per the project's tmp\n  symlink convention).\n\nEach entry has a sensible default; missing entries fall back to\nthose defaults. The user can override any subset by editing the\nfile.\n\n### File location and format\n\nPath: `config/editor-server.lua` (returns a Lua table) or\n`config/editor-server.json`. Lean toward the Lua table — every\nother config in this project is Lua, and a Lua return-table lets\nthe user compute paths if needed (e.g. `os.getenv(\"HOME\") .. \"/my-libs\"`).\n\nShape:\n\n```lua\nreturn {\n  port = 7474,\n  map_root = \"maps\",\n  asset_dir = \"assets\",\n  bundled_script_dirs = {\n    \"libs\",           -- the in-tree default\n    -- \"~/.soramech/my-libs\",  -- example user override\n  },\n  tmp_dir = \"tmp\",\n}\n```\n\nA startup helper in `src/006-server-main.lua` loads the config,\nfills in defaults, and passes the resolved table down to the HTTP\nserver module. The server prints the resolved config on boot so\nthe user can confirm what's in effect.\n\n### File browser surfacing\n\nThe file browser (issue 211 + 211a) currently lists the map's own\n`src/` and the pipeline-resolved bundled dirs. With this config in\nplace, the bundled list comes from `bundled_script_dirs` directly.\nA second pane (or expandable section per dir) labels each entry by\nits source directory so the user can tell their own bundle apart\nfrom the in-tree `libs/`.\n\n### Why a file, not CLI flags\n\nTwo reasons:\n1. Reproducibility — the config file checks into a personal dotfile\n   or repo, and the editor starts up the same way every time.\n2. Discoverability — a user reading their `config/` directory sees\n   what's customizable. CLI flags are invisible until the user runs\n   `--help`.\n\nCLI flags can layer on top if needed (a `--config-file` override),\nbut the file is the primary mechanism.\n\n### Defaults vs explicit\n\nThe server still works with no config file present — every field\nhas a default and the file is optional. Creating the file is a\n\"customize me\" gesture, not a setup requirement.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Per-map config overrides**: a map could ship its own\n  `config/editor-server.lua` that adds its own bundled dirs. Restart is simpler and\n  matches the existing model. Hot reload is a separate issue if\n  ever wanted.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1.           "content":"# 229 — `read` and `write` box kinds (language-agnostic file IO)\n\n## Status\nopen (redesigned 2026-05-18 — supersedes the earlier \"data source +\nfile_write sink\" proposal kept below for history)\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe `data` kind is recognized by the schema (`call` and `data` are\nthe two valid kinds) and accepted by the loader, but it has no\nruntime semantics distinct from `call`. It carries a `ref` and an\n`fn` like a call box and runs through whichever language driver\nmatches the file extension. The only difference is the green badge\non the canvas — pure cosmetic.\n\n`libs/files.lua::read_text` (issue 216, complete) covers actual\n\"read a text file\" via a regular call box, but only from Lua. A\nBash function that needs file contents has to wire through a Lua\nread box, which is a language-coupling no graph reader expects.\n\n## Intended behavior — three kinds: `call`, `read`, `write`\n\nThree primitive box kinds. `call` is unchanged. `read` and `write`\nare new, dispatch-layer primitives — no language driver runs.\n\n### `read` — file path in, contents out\n\nA `read` box has one input port and one output port:\n\n| port | direction | type   | meaning                            |\n|------|-----------|--------|-------------------------------------|\n| path | in        | string | path to the file on disk            |\n| (single output) | out | string | the file's contents, UTF-8 |\n\nNo `ref`, no `fn`. The dispatch layer reads the file when the box\nfires and pushes the contents onto the output wire.\n\nStatic path option: `read` boxes may also carry a `path` field in\ntheir JSON for the common \"read this fixed file\" case. If the\n`path` input wire is connected, the wire wins; otherwise the JSON\nfield provides the path. (Same override rule wires already follow\nfor literal port values everywhere else.)\n\n### `write` — file path + value in, completion signal out\n\nA `write` box has two input ports and one optional output port:\n\n| port  | direction | type   | meaning                            |\n|-------|-----------|--------|-------------------------------------|\n| path  | in        | string | destination path                    |\n| value | in        | any    | the content to write (see below)    |\n| (single output) | out | boolean | `\"true\"` when the write completed |\n\nThe `value` input is \"any kind\" — whatever comes through the wire\ngets serialized to a UTF-8 string and written to disk. For string\nvalues that means write-as-is; for other types it means a sensible\ntext serialization (JSON-encode if structured, `tostring` if\nprimitive). Defer the bikeshed.\n\nBoth the source and the sink atomic-write where it matters: write\nto `path.tmp`, fsync, rename to `path`. Standard pattern; matches\nhow `soramech-data` handles its writes.\n\n### Schema\n\nFor the source:\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"config\",\n  \"kind\": \"data\",\n  \"path\": \"config.json\",\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 100, \"y\": 100 }\n}\n```\n\n`ref` is gone — repurposed as `path` so the field name says what it\nis at the new abstraction level (read a file at this path, not call\na function at this ref). Inputs are absent; outputs are absent (the\nsingle-output rule still gives one wire).\n\nFor the sink, the kind name TBD; data layout:\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"save\",\n  \"kind\": \"file_write\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    {\"name\": \"path\",  \"type\": \"string\"},\n    {\"name\": \"text\",  \"type\": \"string\"}\n  ],\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 100, \"y\": 100 }\n}\n```\n\nNo `path` field on the box — it's wired in. Lets the user compute\npaths upstream (e.g. by a function that builds a timestamped name).\nCould also add an optional `path` field for the static case where\nthe user just wants a file written to a fixed location.\n\n### Concerns about language-agnostic file IO\n\nThe original \"data files have language semantics\" concern (paraphrasing\nfrom prior conversations: \"different languages store strings\ndifferently\") doesn't apply here. The runtime owns the read/write,\nnot any language; it always emits bytes-as-UTF-8 string and always\naccepts the same shape on the way in. Languages each receive a\nplain string from the wire and turn it into whatever their native\nstring type is — that conversion is already part of the language\nspec contract (issue 303).\n\nThere is one wrinkle: **binary data**. UTF-8 encoding of arbitrary\nbytes can fail (invalid sequences). Two ways to handle:\n1. Reject non-UTF-8 files at read time with a clear error. Forces\n   the user to acknowledge the binary case explicitly.\n2. Pass through as raw bytes in some marker (base64?) and let the\n   downstream box decode. Adds complexity most users won't need.\n\nRecommendation: option 1 for now. Binary data is out of scope\nuntil someone needs it; the error surfaces clearly so the user\ncan switch to a language-specific binary reader.\n\n### JSON parsing\n\nThe user asked whether parsing should happen in the data box or in\na downstream box. Recommendation: **the data box is text-only**;\nJSON parsing belongs to a downstream call (Lua: `dkjson.decode`,\nlanguage-agnostic option: a parse box). Reasons:\n- Parsing a JSON file produces a structured object, not a string;\n  the wire protocol between boxes is currently strings (per the\n  language spec contract). Moving structured values across the\n  wire is a separate change with bigger implications.\n- Different downstream uses want different parsings (decoded\n  table, JSON path extraction, schema validation). Letting the\n  data box stay narrow keeps it composable.\n\n## Migration\n\nExisting `data` boxes (if any) currently behave like `call`. They\nhave a `ref` and `fn`. Two options:\n1. Convert `data` → `call` for old boxes, then redefine `data` as\n   the new file-source shape.\n2. Leave old `data` boxes as-is; the editor refuses to interpret\n   them as the new shape until the user explicitly converts.\n\nOption 1 is cleaner since the existing usage was incidental\n(nobody was treating `data` as semantically distinct). A small\nmigration in `src/003-loader.lua` rewrites old `data` boxes on\nread.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Schema** (`src/001-schema.lua`): allow `data` boxes with\n   `path` and no `ref`/`fn`; the new kind for writes (TBD name)\n   takes inputs `path` and `text` and no `ref`/`fn`.\n2. **Loader** (`src/003-loader.lua`): convert legacy `data` boxes\n   (`kind=data` with `ref`/`fn`) to `kind=call`. Validate the new\n   shapes.\n3. **Phase 2 executor** (`src/004-executor.lua`): handle the new\n   kinds directly — read the file and push to output for the\n   source; receive inputs and write to disk for the sink. No\n   driver invocation either way.\n4. **Phase 3 dispatch** (issue 304): same handling at the dispatch\n   layer. Source and sink are dispatch-layer primitives, alongside\n   iterator and comparator routing.\n5. **Inspector** (`assets/js/004-inspector.js`): when `kind=data`,\n   show a `path` text input in place of `ref`/`fn`/inputs. When\n   `kind=file_write` (or final name), show the inputs section as\n   usual but no ref/fn/output.\n6. **Box rendering** (`assets/js/002-boxes.js`): keep the green\n   badge for the source; pick a color for the sink.\n7. **Documentation**: update `docs/001-architecture.md` to describe\n   the new `data` semantics. The old \"library box\" notes (if any)\n   need a small rewrite.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Sink kind name**: `file_write`, `write`, `out`, `save`,\n  `to_file`, `sink`. Lean toward `file_write` for \"says what it is.\"\n- **Static vs wired path on the sink**: support both, or pick one?\n  Wired path is more flexible; static path is a common case worth\n  one fewer wire. Probably accept both — `path` in the box JSON\n  is used as the default; if a wire is connected to the `path`\n  input, it overrides.\n- **Binary data**: explicitly out of scope per above; revisit when\n  a real use case appears.\n- **Atomic-write vs simple write**: atomic-write (`tmp + rename`)\n  is the safe default. If a user wants log-append semantics,\n  that's a different sink kind (or a flag on this one).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — kind validation, new shape\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — legacy `data` migration\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — phase 2 runtime handling\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — kind-specific inspector layout\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — render\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — update box-kinds section\n- `issues/completed/216-read-file-box.md` — Lua-side equivalent\n  that the language-agnostic source supersedes for primary use\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — phase 3 home for these\n  primitives, alongside iterator and comparator\n- `issues/completed/109-data-files-persistent-and-ephemeral.md`\n  — soramech-data is a separate concern; this issue does not\n  affect it\n",

        "text":"Sure, let me back up.\n\nIssue 236 says **the box header should display the filename of the function the box calls** (its `ref`). E.g. a box pointing at `libs/text.lua::concat` shows `text.lua` in the header.\n\nThat rule works fine for `call` boxes — they have a `ref` pointing at a source file. But the editor has other kinds of boxes too:\n\n- `read` and `write` (new, from updated 229) — no ref, they're dispatch-layer primitives\n- `branch` — predicate routing, no ref\n- `iterator` (issue 221) — loops, no ref\n- `comparator` (the lt/eq/gt output mode) — also has no ref of its own\n\nFor those, there's no filename to put in the header. So *something else* has to go there by default.\n\nIn 236 I left a fallback rule: \"if there's no ref, use the kind name.\" That means a `read` box's header would just say `read`, a `branch` would say `branch`, etc. Functional, but kind of bland — and somebody has to decide whether `read`'s header should say `\"read\"` or `\"read file\"` or just an icon, etc.\n\n**That decision — what each kind's default header text is — needs to live somewhere.** It's a one-line-per-kind lookup table:\n\n| kind | default header |\n|------|---------------|\n| call | (basename of ref) |\n| read | \"read\" |\n| write | \"write\" |\n| branch | \"branch\" |\n| iterator | \"iter\" |\n| comparator | \"?\" |\n\nMy question was: do you want me to **pick those default strings now** and write them into 236 (or into a new tiny issue), or **leave it open** for whoever implements 236 to pick on the fly?\n\nEither is fine — I just wanted to flag that the table doesn't exist yet and somebody will have to fill it in."

        "content":"1\t// Box rendering, layout, and hit testing.\n2\t// Each box knows its world-space position; the camera transform is applied by the canvas.\n3\t\n4\tconst Boxes = (() => {\n5\t  const BOX_W         = 180;\n6\t  const BOX_HEADER    = 36;\n7\t  const PORT_ROW_H    = 22;\n8\t  const PORT_R        = 6;   // port dot radius in world units\n9\t  const MIN_BOX_H     = 80;\n10\t\n11\t  const KIND_COLOR = { call: '#4a9eff', data: '#4caf7d' };\n12\t\n13\t  // Comparator branch colors: lt=orange, eq=blue, gt=green\n14\t  const BRANCH_COLOR = { lt: '#ff8c42', eq: '#4a9eff', gt: '#4caf7d' };\n15\t\n16\t  // boxes: { [id]: box_data }\n17\t  let boxes = {};\n18\t\n19\t  // {{{ box_height\n20\t  function box_height(box) {\n21\t    const n_in  = (box.inputs || []).length;\n22\t    // Output rows: iterator boxes have N named slots (issue 221);\n23\t    // comparator active: 3 dots (lt/eq/gt); sink: 0; otherwise 1.\n24\t    let n_out;\n25\t    if (box.iterator_outputs) {\n26\t      n_out = box.iterator_outputs.length;\n27\t    } else if (box.has_output === false) {\n28\t      n_out = 0;\n29\t    } else if (box.comparand && box.comparand !== '') {\n30\t      n_out = 3;\n31\t    } else {\n32\t      n_out = 1;\n33\t    }\n34\t    return Math.max(MIN_BOX_H, BOX_HEADER + Math.max(n_in, n_out) * PORT_ROW_H + 8);\n35\t  }\n36\t  // }}}\n37\t\n38\t  // {{{ port_positions\n39\t  // Returns world-space {x,y} for each port dot on a box.\n40\t  // Output side: null-named single dot when no comparand; 'lt'/'eq'/'gt' dots when comparand set.\n41\t  function port_positions(box) {\n42\t    const bx = box.ui?.x ?? 0;\n43\t    const by = box.ui?.y ?? 0;\n44\t    const h  = box_height(box);\n45\t    const inputs = box.inputs || [];\n46\t\n47\t    const in_pts = inputs.map((p, i) => ({\n48\t      name: p.name, side: 'input',\n49\t      x: bx,\n50\t      y: by + BOX_HEADER + PORT_ROW_H * i + PORT_ROW_H / 2,\n51\t    }));\n52\t\n53\t    let out_pts;\n54\t    if (box.has_output === false) {\n55\t      // sink box — function has no return values (issue 226). No output\n56\t      // port, no wire-grab target, nothing for the inspector to render.\n57\t      out_pts = [];\n58\t    } else if (box.iterator_outputs) {\n59\t      // iterator box (issue 221) — N named output dots stacked down\n60\t      // the right edge, one per declared slot. Slot names land in the\n61\t      // `name` field, so the wire's `from_branch` will pick them up\n62\t      // exactly like a comparator branch name.\n63\t      out_pts = box.iterator_outputs.map((slot, i) => ({\n64\t        name: slot, side: 'output',\n65\t        x: bx + BOX_W,\n66\t        y: by + BOX_HEADER + PORT_ROW_H * i + PORT_ROW_H / 2,\n67\t      }));\n68\t    } else if (box.comparand && box.comparand !== '') {\n69\t      // three comparator dots\n70\t      out_pts = ['lt', 'eq', 'gt'].map((branch, i) => ({\n71\t        name: branch, side: 'output',\n72\t        x: bx + BOX_W,\n73\t        y: by + BOX_HEADER + PORT_ROW_H * i + PORT_ROW_H / 2,\n74\t      }));\n75\t    } else {\n76\t      // single output dot, vertically centered in the box\n77\t      out_pts = [{\n78\t        name: null, side: 'output',\n79\t        x: bx + BOX_W,\n80\t        y: by + h / 2,\n81\t      }];\n82\t    }\n83\t\n84\t    return { inputs: in_pts, outputs: out_pts };\n85\t  }\n86\t  // }}}\n87\t\n88\t  // {{{ draw_box\n89\t  function draw_box(ctx, box, selected) {\n90\t    const x = box.ui?.x ?? 0;\n91\t    const y = box.ui?.y ?? 0;\n92\t    const w = BOX_W;\n93\t    const h = box_height(box);\n94\t    const kind  = box.kind || 'call';\n95\t    const color = KIND_COLOR[kind] || '#888';\n96\t\n97\t    // shadow when selected\n98\t    if (selected) {\n99\t      ctx.shadowColor = color;\n100\t      ctx.shadowBlur  = 12;\n101\t    }\n102\t\n103\t    // body\n104\t    ctx.fillStyle   = '#1e2130';\n105\t    ctx.strokeStyle = selected ?
