Different file → label snaps\nto the new basename, matching the canvas-header convention.\n\nTested with the 10-case node script (call w/ ref+fn, label\noverride, every non-call kind, unknown kind, missing kind →\nid fallback, branch name preserved as output label). User\nverified visually.",
    "originalFile":"# 236 — Box header shows filename; output label shows `fn_name()` call form\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA call box's header (the bold text at the top of the box on the\ncanvas) currently displays the box's label — by default, the\nfunction name (e.g. `concat`, `read_text`, `prompt_ollama`). The\noutput port on the right edge has a generic label (`output` /\n`result` / whatever the parser produced).\n\nFor a user reading a map, the header gives one of the two pieces\nof relevant identity (the function), but the other piece — *which\nfile the function comes from* — is missing from the visible box.\nYou can see `concat` and not know whether it is `libs/text.lua`'s\nconcat or some other module's concat without opening the inspector\nand reading `ref`.\n\nThe single output label, `output`, is generic and conveys nothing\nabout what's being computed.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nReinterpret the two text slots on a box:\n\n- **Box header (top)** = the **filename** of `ref` (basename, no\n  path prefix, e.g. `text.lua`). This is the module / file the\n  function lives in.\n- **Output port label (right edge)** = the function call form,\n  `fn_name()`, e.g. `concat()`, `read_text()`, `prompt_ollama()`.\n  This reads as \"this wire carries the return value of calling\n  fn_name.\"\n\nSo a box that calls `concat` from `libs/text.lua` reads, top to\nbottom on the canvas:\n\n```\n┌─ text.lua ────────────────┐\n│ ● sep      \"\\n\\n\"          │\n│ ● text_0                   │   concat() ●\n│ ● text_1                   │\n└────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\n(Combined with issue 235, the `sep` literal also shows on the\ncanvas — included here for illustration of how the canvas reads as\na whole.)\n\n### Why this split\n\nA reader scanning a map mentally parses it as a series of function\ncalls. The function call form `fn_name()` is the natural way to\nread \"this is the value of calling fn_name with these inputs.\" The\nfilename header sits one layer up: \"this function comes from this\nmodule.\" Together they read like an annotated call site — module\non top, return value on the side.\n\nIt also frees the box header from having to be unique. Right now\nthe default label is the function name, which collides across\nboxes that all call the same function. The filename groups by\nmodule — many boxes can share `text.lua` as their header and that\nis fine; what distinguishes them is what they compute and how\nthey are wired.\n\n### Label override\n\nThe user-editable `box.label` field remains. If a user sets an\nexplicit label, it overrides the filename in the header. Use case:\nmultiple boxes in the same map call `text.concat`, and the user\nwants to name them by their role (\"join paragraphs\", \"join CSV\nrow\") rather than by module. The override is intentional and only\napplied when set; default behavior is filename-from-ref.\n\nThe output port label is not user-editable in this issue — it is\nalways derived from `fn`. (If a use case appears, add it later.)\n\n### Filename derivation\n\n`ref` is a path like `libs/text.lua` or `maps/foo/src/echo.sh`.\nTake the basename (`text.lua`, `echo.sh`). Do not strip the\nextension — the extension says which language driver runs, which\nis information the user cares about.\n\nFor boxes without a `ref` (branch boxes, comparators, the `read`\nand `write` primitives from issue 229, iterators from issue 221),\nthe header shows the **full kind name** in plain text. No\nabbreviations.\n\n| kind        | default header text |\n|-------------|---------------------|\n| `call`      | basename of `ref`   |\n| `read`      | `read`              |\n| `write`     | `write`             |\n| `branch`    | `branch`            |\n| `iterator`  | `iterator`          |\n| `comparator`| `comparator`        |\n\nThe user-set `box.label` override still wins above all of these —\nthe table is the default for \"no override, no ref.\"\n\nThese boxes also skip the `fn()` output label (which only applies\nto `call`). Use a per-kind output name instead:\n\n| kind        | output label |\n|-------------|--------------|\n| `read`      | `contents`   |\n| `write`     | `done`       |\n| `branch`    | (multiple ports, named by branch) |\n| `iterator`  | `item`       |\n| `comparator`| `lt` / `eq` / `gt` (three ports) |\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `assets/js/002-boxes.js::draw_box` — header text path:\n   - If `box.label` is set and non-empty, use it (current behavior).\n   - Else, derive from `box.ref`: basename of the path string.\n   - Else (no ref), use `box.kind` as a final fallback.\n2. Output port label path: when `box.fn` is set, render\n   `${box.fn}()` instead of `output` / `result`. Otherwise leave\n   the existing default.\n3. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — the inspector's \"label\" field\n   shows the override value (the explicit user-set label) and its\n   placeholder shows what the canvas is using by default. So the\n   user sees \"currently displayed: text.lua (from ref)\" and can\n   override.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Path vs basename for the header**: a deeply-nested ref like\n  `maps/foo/src/sub/echo.sh` becomes just `echo.sh` in the header.\n  Is the parent dir worth keeping (`sub/echo.sh`) for disambiguation?\n  Probably not by default — the inspector shows the full ref —\n  but worth revisiting if collisions cause confusion.\n- **Future kinds**: when a new kind is added later, it picks up\n  the same convention — full kind name as the default header,\n  per-kind output label. Add one row to each table above.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box draw routine\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — label field + placeholder hint\n- `issues/completed/207-source-file-browser-and-port-auto-population.md`\n  — ref/fn pairing established here\n- `issues/completed/210-llm-route-box.md` — single-output redesign\n  this issue's `fn()` label leans on\n- `issues/235-literal-value-replaces-port-name-on-canvas.md` — sister\n  display change for input ports\n",

        "input":{
          "command":"git commit -m \"$(cat <<'EOF'\nFilename headers and fn() return-value labels on every box (issue 236)\n\nA reader scanning a map now sees what each box actually does\nwithout clicking through to the inspector. The box header tells\nyou what module the function lives in — the source file's name,\ndisplayed in place of the auto-assigned id — and the right-side\noutput dot is annotated with the function's call form, so a wire\nleaving a box reads as the return value of that call. Branching\noutputs (the lt/eq/gt fan-out, the iterator's named slots) keep\ntheir existing labels.\n\nPicking a function via the file browser also keeps the header\nhonest: choosing a function from a different file overwrites the\nheader with the new filename, while switching between functions\ninside the same file leaves whatever label the user had typed\nalone. A user-set label always trumps the default — the\ninspector's title field accepts an explicit override and shows\nthe would-be-default as its placeholder so you can see exactly\nwhat would render if you cleared the field.\n\nNon-call kinds (branch, comparator, iterator, data) fall back to\nthe kind's plain name in the header so future kinds add one row\nto a small lookup table and Just Work.\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\"",
          "description":"Commit issue 236"
        }
      }],
    "role":"assistant",

          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"Edge cases:\n- `nil` text → empty array\n- `nil` or empty `sep` → single-element array containing the whole input\n  (avoids an infinite loop and matches common library behavior)\n- Separator characters that are also Lua-pattern metacharacters (`.`,\n  `*`, `[`, etc.) are matched literally — `string.find` is called with\n  `plain = true`.\n\n---\n\n## M.upper(text) → string\n\nUpper-cased copy of `text`. `nil` text returns the empty string.\n\n## M.lower(text) → string\n\nLower-cased copy of `text`. `nil` text returns the empty string.\n\n## M.trim(text) → string\n\nStrips leading and trailing whitespace (the `%s` class — spaces,\ntabs, newlines, etc). Whitespace inside the string is preserved.\n\n## M.replace(text, find, repl) → string\n\nReturns `text` with every occurrence of `find` replaced by `repl`.\nPlain-string match; `find` may contain any characters without\nescaping. Empty `find` returns the text unchanged.\n\n## M.replace_first(text, find, repl) → string\n\nSame as `M.replace` but stops after the first occurrence. Two\nfunctions instead of a flag because the editor has no boolean-port\nprimitive yet — picking by function name is clearer than a third\ninput that takes the string `\"true\"`.\n\n## M.contains(text, needle) → boolean\n\nTrue if `needle` appears anywhere in `text`. Empty needle returns\n**false** (asking \"does it contain nothing?\" is meaningless;\nreturning true would silently short-circuit guards).\n\n## M.starts_with(text, prefix) → boolean\n\nTrue if `text` begins with `prefix`. Empty prefix returns true\n(every string begins with the empty string — matches the\nconventional set-theoretic answer).\n\n## M.ends_with(text, suffix) → boolean\n\nTrue if `text` ends with `suffix`. Empty suffix returns true,\nsame reason as `starts_with`.\n\n## M.length(text) → integer\n\nNumber of bytes in `text` (Lua's `#` operator). For UTF-8 input\nthis is the byte length, not the character count — wide\ncharacters count as multiple bytes.\n\n## M.substring(text, start, len) → string\n\nSlice of `text` starting at 1-indexed `start`. If `len` is\nomitted, takes everything from `start` to the end. Out-of-range\npositions follow `string.sub` semantics — clamped, not errored.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/libs/text.lua.info.md"
        }
      }],

          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"# 237 — Expand the bundled string-manipulation library\n\n## Status\ncomplete\n\n## Implementation notes\n\nTen new functions appended to `libs/text.lua` after the existing\n`concat` and `split`: `upper`, `lower`, `trim`, `replace`,\n`replace_first`, `contains`, `starts_with`, `ends_with`,\n`length`, `substring`. The information file\n`libs/text.lua.info.md` carries one short entry per function in\nthe same shape as the existing `concat` / `split` rows.\n\nTwo design specifics worth keeping:\n\n- All matching is **plain string**, never Lua pattern. The\n  `find`/`prefix`/`suffix` arguments may carry any characters\n  without escaping. `replace` / `replace_first` use a private\n  `replace_n` helper that walks the input with\n  `string.find(..., plain=true)` and emits an interleaved slice +\n  replacement list, sidestepping the otherwise-needed\n  pattern-metacharacter escape pass for both the search needle\n  and the replacement.\n- Booleans cross the wire as real JSON booleans, not as the\n  strings `\"true\"` / `\"false\"`, because the Lua driver does\n  `json.encode(result)`. The info.md spells this out so a user\n  doesn't expect string-formatted booleans when wiring\n  `contains` / `starts_with` / `ends_with` into a downstream\n  consumer.\n\nTested via a 28-case luajit script covering each function plus\n`nil` and edge inputs (empty string args, out-of-range\nsubstring, pattern-metacharacter haystacks for `replace`, etc).\nThe file browser picks all twelve public functions up via the\nexisting `function M.<name>` parser — no editor-side changes\nneeded since the bundled-dirs work in issue 238 already makes\n`libs/` visible to every map.",

    "originalFile":"# 237 — Expand the bundled string-manipulation library\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`libs/text.lua` (created in issue 217) exposes two functions:\n\n- `M.concat(sep, ...)` — variadic join with a separator\n- `M.split(text, sep)` — split a string on a plain separator,\n  returns a JSON-encoded array\n\nThat covers two of the most common string operations and was\ndeliberately minimal — just enough for the demo map that drove 217.\nA user wanting to upper-case, lower-case, find-and-replace, trim,\nor substring has to either write the function themselves into a\nproject-local file, or fall back to a Lua call box pointing at\n`string.upper` / `string.gsub` directly (which works but is more\ntyping per box).\n\nThere is also no canonical home for \"the string library that ships\nwith the editor.\" `libs/text.lua` exists but its scope was set by\none issue's needs, not by a broader plan.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n`libs/text.lua` grows into a small, opinionated standard library\nof string operations, each wired to be variadic-friendly and\nsingle-output where it makes sense. The full set in this issue:\n\n| function                          | inputs                          | output                          |\n|-----------------------------------|----------------------------------|---------------------------------|\n| `M.concat(sep, ...)`              | sep, variadic text               | joined string (already exists)  |\n| `M.split(text, sep)`              | text, sep                        | JSON array of parts (exists)    |\n| `M.upper(text)`                   | text                             | upper-cased string              |\n| `M.lower(text)`                   | text                             | lower-cased string              |\n| `M.trim(text)`                    | text                             | leading + trailing ws stripped  |\n| `M.replace(text, find, repl)`     | text, find, repl                 | every occurrence replaced       |\n| `M.replace_first(text, find, repl)`| text, find, repl                | first occurrence only           |\n| `M.contains(text, needle)`        | text, needle                     | boolean (as `\"true\"`/`\"false\"`) |\n| `M.starts_with(text, prefix)`     | text, prefix                     | boolean                         |\n| `M.ends_with(text, suffix)`       | text, suffix                     | boolean                         |\n| `M.length(text)`                  | text                             | integer (as string on wire)     |\n| `M.substring(text, start, len)`   | text, start, len (1-indexed)     | substring                       |\n\nAll `find` / `prefix` / `suffix` arguments are **plain strings**,\nnot Lua patterns — same convention as `M.split`. A user who wants\npatterns can call `string.gsub` directly via a call box. The\nlibrary's job is \"common case, no surprises.\"\n\n`M.replace_first` is a separate function rather than a flag on\n`replace` because the editor has no boolean-port primitive yet\n(literal values are strings; \"all or first\" toggles cleanly\nbetween two function names). Could collapse later when a primitive\nboolean exists.\n\n### Companion info.md\n\nUpdate `libs/text.lua.info.md` so each function gets its own entry\nwith inputs / outputs / one-line description. Issue 207's file\nbrowser parses signatures from source; the info.md is the\nhuman-skim version. (Per CLAUDE.md: prefer reading info.md over\nsource for an overview.)\n\n### Why these specifically\n\nSkim a handful of maps and the same operations show up: cleaning\ninput (trim), normalizing case (upper / lower), simple\nsubstitution (replace), boolean guards (contains / starts_with /\nends_with), array slicing (substring). The list above covers the\n\"would you have written this as a helper anyway?\" cases without\nsprawling into a kitchen-sink std lib.\n\nOperations explicitly **not** in this issue:\n\n- Regex / pattern matching — a separate `libs/regex.lua` issue.\n  Pattern syntax is its own UI problem (which dialect? escape\n  rules?) and deserves a dedicated home.\n- Encode / decode (base64, URL, hex) — separate `libs/codec.lua`.\n- Format strings (`printf`-style) — single-output-wire constraint\n  makes the call shape awkward; revisit when the language spec for\n  format string handling firms up.\n\n### Bundled location convention\n\nFiles in `libs/` are the bundled, edit-as-default modules every\nmap can `ref` directly without per-map setup. This issue does not\nchange that — it just fills out one of those bundled modules.\n\nA future per-language convention (issue 303 territory) might split\n`libs/` by language (`libs/lua/text.lua`, `libs/c/text.c`,\n`libs/bash/text.sh`). Today everything in `libs/` is Lua; revisit\nthe split when a second language ships a bundled standard library.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `libs/text.lua` — append the new functions. Each is a 1-3 line\n   wrapper over a `string.*` builtin or a small primitive. Keep\n   them order-aligned with the table above for readability.\n2. `libs/text.lua.info.md` — add one entry per new function\n   following the existing format. Include the \"plain string, not\n   pattern\" note where applicable.\n3. A small test map (`tests/maps/text-lib/`?) — one box per\n   function, hand-traced expected outputs. The phase-2 integration\n   tests can pick it up automatically (issue 311 wiring).\n4. The demo for the current phase should pick up at least one or\n   two of these on its display path so the user sees the library\n   in action.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `libs/text.lua` — host of the new functions\n- `libs/text.lua.info.md` — documentation companion\n- `issues/completed/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — founded\n  this library with concat + split\n- `issues/238-editor-http-server-config-file.md` — paired issue\n  that makes \"where do bundled libs live\" configurable, so a user\n  can add their own bundled-default directory alongside `libs/`\n",

    "originalFile":"# 234 — Middle-click duplicates the selected box (with wires)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA box on the canvas can be selected (single click) and edited via\nthe inspector, but there is no shortcut for \"make me another one\njust like this.\" A user who wants to repeat a configured box has\nto:\n\n1. Right-click → \"add box here\" to spawn a fresh empty box.\n2. Reopen the file browser, re-pick the same ref / fn.\n3. Re-type all the literal input values.\n4. Re-wire every upstream connection by hand.\n\nFor a box with several literal values and several incoming wires\nthis is many clicks of pure repetition, and any one of them is a\nchance to typo a value or miss a wire.\n\nMiddle-mouse currently has no editor behavior other than the\nbrowser's default scroll-anchor (which is itself disruptive on a\ncanvas app).\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n**When a box is selected and the user does a short middle-mouse\nclick (not a drag) anywhere on the canvas**, the editor creates a\nduplicate of the selected box at the cursor position. The duplicate\ncarries over:\n\n- `ref`, `fn`, `kind`, `outputs`, `variadic_inputs` — same function\n  bound to the new box.\n- Every input port, including its literal value (if any).\n- Every wire whose destination is the original box: a matching wire\n  is created from the same source box / output to the new box's\n  same-named input. Outgoing wires (where the original is the\n  source) are NOT duplicated — multiple boxes fanning out from one\n  source is the normal case; multiple boxes converging on the same\n  downstream port is not.\n\nThe duplicate gets a fresh `id` and a `ui.x / ui.y` at the cursor\nlocation. The label is the original's label suffixed `(copy)` (or\n`(copy 2)`, `(copy 3)` if the suffix is already present) — same\nnaming pattern most desktop UIs use.\n\nA middle-drag (the cursor moved more than a few pixels between\npress and release) is not a duplicate. Reserve that gesture for\nfuture pan / other use; for now it is a no-op rather than an\naccidental copy.\n\nIf no box is selected, middle-click is a no-op (with maybe a\ntoast / status hint, \"select a box to duplicate it\").\n\n### Why middle-click\n\nRight-click already opens the context menu (issue 212). Left-click\nselects / deselects. Middle-click is the only unused primary\nbutton, and the \"click on empty canvas to place\" muscle memory from\nadd-box mode transfers cleanly: select source → middle-click target.\n\n### Why duplicate incoming wires by default\n\nThe whole reason to duplicate is \"I want another node fed by the\nsame data.\" Forcing the user to re-wire defeats the gesture.\nOutgoing wires are skipped because the user usually wants the copy\nto feed something *new* downstream — that's the half they're about\nto wire up.\n\n### Open question — duplicate-with-no-wires variant?\n\nHold a modifier (`Shift+middle-click`?) to duplicate without\nwires? Defer until someone asks; the wireless version is just \"add\na fresh box and browse to the same fn,\" which the right-click menu\nalready covers.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `assets/js/005-app.js` — middle-mouse handlers:\n   - `mousedown` (button 1): record press position + selected box id.\n   - `mouseup` (button 1): if movement ≤ threshold and a box is\n     selected, call `duplicate_box(selected_id, cursor_world_pos)`.\n   - `preventDefault` on the mousedown to suppress browser\n     scroll-anchor behavior.\n2. New module function `Boxes.duplicate(src_box, x, y)`:\n   - Clone the box JSON, assign a new id, set `ui.x/ui.y`.\n   - Suffix the label with `(copy)` / `(copy N)`.\n   - POST to the server (existing create-box endpoint).\n3. Wire duplication: iterate every connection in the map whose\n   `to_box == src_box.id`. For each, POST a matching connection\n   with `to_box = new_box.id` (same `to_input`, same\n   `from_box` / `from_output`).\n4. Update local Boxes cache and re-render. Select the new box so\n   the user can immediately edit / nudge it.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/005-app.js` — pointer event handlers, current\n  right-click context menu lives here.\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — local box cache + create flow.\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — `create_connection`, wire data model.\n- `src/005-http-server.lua` — existing POST endpoints for boxes\n  and connections.\n- `issues/completed/212-editor-interaction-modes.md` — established\n  the right-click and tool-mode patterns this issue extends.\n",

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Here's where we stand:\n\n**Code today**: `data` is recognized by the schema as a valid `kind` (alongside `call`) and offered in the inspector's kind dropdown, but it has **no distinct runtime semantics** — the executor treats it like a `call` box. The only difference is the green badge color on the canvas. Functionally cosmetic.\n\n**Issue 229 (open)**: I redesigned the spec earlier to replace `data` with two dispatch-layer primitives — `read` (path → contents) and `write` (path + value → done signal). Neither is implemented yet. The design hasn't included a \"literal output value\" mode.\n\n**What you're proposing** is a third mode I hadn't captured in 229: the data box itself can carry an inline literal output value. Logic:\n\n- If a literal `output_value` is set in the inspector → emit that directly, no I/O.\n- Else if a `path` input is supplied (wire or literal) → read the file at path and emit its contents.\n- Else → error.\n\nThis is the same precedence rule input ports already follow (wire > literal value), just applied to the output side. Same mental model.\n\nThis is a nicer design than 229's current \"two separate kinds\" approach in one important way: a user who just wants to drop a small inline config value into a graph (a port, a prompt, a constant) doesn't need a real file at all — they type it into the inspector and that's the box. If they later want to externalize it, they can swap the literal for a `path` input pointing at a file.\n\n**Decision point**: do you want me to **redesign 229** around this single-`data`-kind-with-literal-or-file behavior (keeping `write` as a separate sink kind, since it really is a different concern), or **leave 229 as-is and open a new issue** for \"literal output on data boxes\" as a smaller, separately-implementable feature on top?\n\nMy recommendation: update 229 in place. The literal-output idea subsumes the `read` half cleanly, and you've already once-redesigned 229 in this conversation — the design history thread stays on one ticket."

## [898]

```json
{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-19T17:18:09.345Z",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "uuid":"a0bd82c3-00e9-4382-a3c9-d460e2c6a537",
  "parentUuid":"4f2fb37e-e54b-4299-83fe-e857508cbd3c",
  "sessionId":"8fe72ba4-53d6-481c-9958-56808ae4f711",

  "isSidechain":false,

  "requestId":"req_011CbCMj9o7hxKcM86syrvKD",
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"You can combine all three — the question is whether the cost is worth it. Here's where the edges are:\n\n**1. Two ways to source the output → which wins?**\nIf a box has both a literal output value AND a file path configured, the output port has two possible sources. You'd need a precedence rule (literal beats file, or vice versa) and the user has to remember it. The input-port rule today is \"wire beats literal\" — extending that to outputs is consistent but not obvious at a glance.\n\n**2. Read and write share the same `path`.**\nIf the box has a `path` configured AND a `write_value` wire AND no output literal, is it reading or writing? You'd pick by presence of `write_value` — wire connected → write mode, no wire → read mode. Workable, but a user who *forgets* to wire the `write_value` ends up with a silent read of the destination file they meant to write to. That's a real footgun.\n\n**3. The output port means different things in each mode.**\n- Read mode → emits file contents (possibly large text).\n- Write mode → emits `true` / done.\n- Literal mode → emits whatever the user typed.\n\nDownstream boxes wired to that port can't statically tell what kind of value is flowing through — same wire, three different semantics. A reader scanning the map sees one node shape but has to read the configuration to know what it does.\n\n**4. Validation surface blows up.**\nThree kinds today = three fixed shapes the validator checks. One unified kind = 2³ combinations of (literal? path? write_value?) the validator has to either accept or reject with a clear rule per combo. More edge-case bugs hide there.\n\n**5. Canvas identity disappears.**\nToday a green data box looks different from a blue call box at a glance. If one kind can be source-or-sink-or-constant, the badge stops telling the reader what's happening — they have to open the inspector.\n\n---\n\n**A middle ground I'd recommend**: split exactly along the natural seam — *sourcing* vs *sinking*.\n\n- **`data` (source)** — emits one value. The value comes from either an inline literal typed in the inspector OR a file read at `path` (literal or wired). Same output port, same semantics: \"here is the value.\" Choosing literal vs file is a low-stakes mode toggle because both end up as the same kind of thing on the wire.\n\n- **`write` (sink)** — writes an input value to disk at `path`. Emits a done signal. Different action, different look on the canvas.\n\nThis collapses your three asks into two kinds while keeping the \"I just want to type a value into a box\" use case as a first-class feature of the source kind. Reading and emit-literal sit comfortably in one box because they answer the same question. Writing is its own thing because it does something fundamentally different (mutates the filesystem).\n\nWant me to update 229 around that two-kind design (`data` with literal-or-file + `write`)?"
      }],

Can we make write be an orange cheddar color? nice and vivid but on the darker side.\n\nread should hide / disable it's input port if a literal value is entered in the inspector.\n\nread should detect the language used by each of it's output wires - remember, each output port can have multiple wires coming out of it. If there's multiple just do them in a for loop, for each wire. the downstream boxes should treat all read boxes as native.\n\nwrite should do similar - it should detect which language the input wire is coming from, and use the correct writing procedure defined in the language spec to reduce the friction.",

We require\nboth so any language can play any role.\n\nSpecs that haven't been updated yet should set both callbacks\nto a stub that returns -1 with a clear error message (\"spec\n`<name>`: native_to_json not implemented; this box's value\ncan't be routed cross-language\"). The hard-fail makes the gap\nloud rather than producing wrong output.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. Extend the `lang_spec_t` declaration in\n   `langs/lang-spec.h` if not already done by 312's\n   infrastructure work. (Per the round summary, the slot is\n   reserved.)\n2. Implement `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` in each\n   spec:\n   - **Lua spec**: walk the value at the stack index. Use the\n     existing C JSON writer (`libs/json/json.c`). Handle Lua\n     tables both as arrays (1-indexed contiguous integer keys)\n     and as objects. Refuse functions, userdata, threads.\n   - **C spec**: depends on 307's typed-wrapper machinery. For\n     now, a stub that only supports scalar types (int, double,\n     string) is enough to get data boxes working in C.\n   - **Bash spec**: validate-and-pass-through. The script is\n     expected to produce JSON. `native_to_json` runs the JSON\n     parser to validate; `json_to_native` is identity.\n3. Extend the data box runtime path in `src/012-dispatch.c`\n   (or wherever data boxes dispatch from) to consult `lang` /\n   `ref` when set and route through the spec callback chain.\n4. Add a fixture: `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` with a Lua\n   data box, a C consumer, and a Bash consumer all reading the\n   same value. The integration check asserts each consumer\n   sees the right data.\n5. Update each spec's `*.info.md` to document the native handle\n   shape its callbacks expect.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — extend the contract\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n  implement the callbacks\n- `langs/{lua,c,bash}/spec.info.md` — document native handle\n  semantics per spec\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — data-box dispatch path\n- `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` — new fixture (see step 4)\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — same author-writes-natural-\n  code principle; this issue extends it from call boxes to data\n  boxes\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — reuses the same\n  spec callbacks for a different (performance) reason\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Bash's `json_to_native` is a near-identity because the\n  scripts already deal in text. Is there value in having it\n  validate and reformat for consistency? Probably yes; cheap\n  insurance against malformed downstream input.\n- Should the Lua spec auto-detect array-vs-object tables, or\n  require the box author to annotate? Auto-detect (contiguous\n  1-indexed integer keys → array; otherwise object) is what\n  every other lua-to-json library does and is intuitive enough.\n- C spec's `native_to_json` for arbitrary structs is a real\n  rabbit hole. Tie scope to 307 — the same type declarations\n  drive both the wrapper and the JSON walk. Until 307 lands,\n  only scalar types are supported for C data boxes.\n",
      "totalLines":237,

          "content":"# 229 — `read` and `write` box kinds (language-aware file IO)\n\n## Status\nopen (redesigned 2026-05-19 — supersedes the earlier \"data source +\nfile_write sink\" and the still-earlier \"data kind / literal-or-file\nunified source\" proposals, both kept below for history)\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe `data` kind is recognized by the schema and accepted by the\nloader, but has no runtime semantics distinct from `call`. It\ncarries `ref` and `fn` like a call box and runs through whichever\nlanguage driver matches the file extension. The green badge on\nthe canvas is purely cosmetic — the box behaves exactly like\n`call`.\n\n`libs/files.lua::read_text` and friends cover the actual \"read a\ntext file\" case (issue 216, complete) via regular call boxes,\nbut only from Lua. A Bash function that needs file contents has\nto wire through a Lua read box, which is a language-coupling no\ngraph reader expects.\n\n## Intended behavior — two kinds, `read` and `write`\n\nBoth are dispatch-layer primitives — no language driver runs for\ntheir core IO. The language specs DO participate at the wire\nboundary so the value crosses cross-language seams natively (see\n\"language-aware IO\" below). The phase-3 entry point lives in\n`src/012-dispatch.c`; the phase-2 mirror lives in\n`src/004-executor.lua` so the editor's \"test run\" works the same.\n\n### `read` — emits a value\n\nA `read` box has one input port and one output port. The output\nis **always trusted to produce a value** — that's the box's\nsingle job, and downstream consumers can rely on it.\n\n| port | direction | type   | meaning                            |\n|------|-----------|--------|-------------------------------------|\n| path | in        | string | path to the file on disk            |\n| (single output) | out | any | the value to emit                 |\n\nNo `ref`, no `fn`. The box decides what to emit using this\nprecedence:\n\n1. If the inspector carries an **inline literal value** for the\n   box, emit that directly. **The `path` input port hides on the\n   canvas** in this mode — there's no file involved, and a path\n   port on a box that doesn't read a file would just confuse the\n   reader.\n2. Else if `path` is supplied (via wire or via an inline literal\n   path on the input port), read that file from disk and emit its\n   contents.\n3. Else error — a `read` with neither a literal nor a path is a\n   misconfiguration the validator should catch.\n\n### `write` — emits a done signal\n\n| port  | direction | type   | meaning                            |\n|-------|-----------|--------|-------------------------------------|\n| path  | in        | string | destination path                    |\n| value | in        | any    | the content to write                |\n| (single output) | out | boolean | `true` when the write completed |\n\nThe output is intentionally minimal — a boolean done signal\nthat downstream graphs can fan into \"and now the file is on\ndisk, fire the next thing\" patterns. It's also easy to ignore\nwhen no one cares: per the unwired-output discard rule\n(documented when this issue lands), a `write` with no wire on\nits output produces the boolean and drops it.\n\nAtomic write: write to `path.tmp`, fsync, rename to `path`.\nSame convention `soramech-data` already uses.\n\n### Canvas colors\n\n- `read` keeps the existing green for data boxes (`#4caf7d`) so\n  source-of-truth-for-a-value boxes read consistently from old\n  maps that still call them `data`.\n- `write` gets **orange cheddar — `#d4762a`** (vivid, dark side,\n  warm). The contrast against `read`'s green makes source vs\n  sink visually obvious at a glance.\n\n### Why two kinds and not one unified `data` box\n\nA previous revision of this issue proposed a single `data` kind\nthat could be source, sink, or constant depending on its\nconfiguration. That collapsed to ambiguity:\n\n- Two ways to source the output (literal vs file) needed a\n  precedence rule.\n- Read and write both want `path` — a \"wrote without meaning to\"\n  footgun lurks when the user forgets to wire `value`.\n- The output port carries fundamentally different semantics by\n  mode (file contents vs done signal vs literal).\n- A canvas reader can't tell what the box does from its shape.\n\nSource vs sink IS the natural seam. `read` always emits a value\n(literal or file). `write` always commits a value to disk.\nDifferent action, different identity, different color.\n\n## Language-aware IO (depends on issue 317)\n\nEvery cross-language seam in the graph goes through the\n`native_to_json` / `json_to_native` callbacks issue 317 adds to\neach `lang_spec_t`. `read` and `write` use that same machinery\nso a Lua data file feeding a C consumer arrives as a native C\nvalue, and a C struct flowing into a `write` is serialized via\nthe C spec rather than blindly stringified by the dispatch\nlayer.\n\n### `read` per-downstream-wire fan-out\n\nA `read` box's single output port can have **N downstream\nwires**, each ending at a box in possibly different languages.\nThe dispatch layer:\n\n1. Sources the value (literal or file bytes).\n2. Iterates the box's outgoing wires. For each:\n   a. Looks up the target box's language via its `ref` extension\n      (or the routing layer's pre-classified `lang` from issue 305).\n   b. Calls that language's `json_to_native` to lift the value\n      into the target language's native form.\n   c. Hands the native value to the target box's input slot.\n\nIf three wires go to a C box, a Lua box, and a Bash box, the\ndispatch loop runs the conversion three times — once per spec.\n**Downstream boxes treat the `read` box's output as native to\ntheir own language.** No SoraMech-specific glue at the consumer.\n\nFor files on disk, `read` treats the file contents as JSON text —\nthe canonical wire format — and feeds those bytes to each\ndownstream spec's `json_to_native`. A Lua user writing a file by\nhand still writes JSON (or uses a `write` box upstream, which\nproduces JSON anyway).\n\n### `write` per-upstream-wire dispatch\n\nA `write` box's `value` input is fed by exactly one upstream\nwire. The dispatch layer:\n\n1. Looks up the source box's language.\n2. Calls that language's `native_to_json` to canonicalize the\n   value to JSON text.\n3. Writes the JSON bytes to `path` atomically.\n\nIf the source is a Lua box returning a table, the Lua spec\nencodes the table to JSON. If the source is a C box returning a\nstruct, the C spec walks the type. The user never sees the\nserialization step — it's the spec's job, not the box author's.\n\n### Why this matters\n\nThe user's mental model is \"I write code in my language, the\ndata crosses the wire, the other side gets it in their\nlanguage.\" `read` and `write` should reinforce that, not break\nit. Either box would otherwise be the place where the user is\nforced to think about JSON shapes, byte order, or string\nescapes. With the spec-driven IO callbacks, all of that lives\nwhere it belongs — in the language specs.\n\n### Dependency relationship with 317\n\n229 cannot land cleanly without 317. The cross-language emit/write\nbehavior described above IS 317's contract; this issue just names\nthe runtime primitives that make first use of it. Implementation\norder: 317 → 229. If 229 lands first with a stub \"everything goes\nthrough bash-style text identity,\" the result is plain string IO\nwith no Lua-table / C-struct support, which is a regression from\nthe design goal.\n\n## Schema\n\n**read** (default file-source form):\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"load_cfg\",\n  \"kind\": \"read\",\n  \"inputs\": [{ \"name\": \"path\" }],\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 100, \"y\": 100 }\n}\n```\n\n**read** with inline literal value (no path port):\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"default_prompt\",\n  \"kind\": \"read\",\n  \"value\": \"You are a helpful assistant.\",\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 100, \"y\": 100 }\n}\n```\n\n**read** with inline literal path (path port still present\non canvas if no `value` is set, but the port's label shows\nthe literal — same convention as issue 235):\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"load_cfg\",\n  \"kind\": \"read\",\n  \"inputs\": [{ \"name\": \"path\", \"value\": \"config.json\" }],\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 100, \"y\": 100 }\n}\n```\n\n**write**:\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"save_result\",\n  \"kind\": \"write\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    { \"name\": \"path\" },\n    { \"name\": \"value\" }\n  ],\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 400, \"y\": 100 }\n}\n```\n\n## Inspector behavior\n\n### `read`\n\n- **Inline value** field (textarea / text input): a free-form\n  literal that, when non-empty, becomes the box's output and\n  HIDES the `path` input port on the canvas. Same hide-when-\n  literal precedence is the obvious progression of issue 235's\n  \"literal value replaces port name\" idea, applied to the port\n  itself.\n- **Path** field: the literal-on-port equivalent for the `path`\n  input. Disabled when the inline value is set.\n- The two fields are mutually-illuminating: typing into one\n  visibly disables the other so the user always knows which\n  mode the box is in.\n\n### `write`\n\n- Two input port rows (`path`, `value`) with the standard\n  port literal / wire UI.\n- No inline-value field (a `write` with no value to commit\n  is meaningless).\n\n### Kind dropdown\n\nReplace the current `['call', 'data']` list with\n`['call', 'read', 'write']`. Picking a kind from this dropdown\nswaps the box's input/output shape per the schemas above.\n\n## Migration\n\nLegacy `data` boxes (the cosmetic-only kind) get rewritten by\nthe loader. Two paths:\n\n- Boxes with a `ref` / `fn` (the call-equivalent shape they\n  carry today) → rewrite `kind` to `call`. Behavior identical\n  to current.\n- Boxes without a `ref` / `fn` (rare — would be invalid today)\n  → rewrite to `read` with no path; the validator then flags\n  them so the user notices and fills in a path or literal.\n\nThe `data` kind is retired entirely. The schema rejects it\nafter migration runs once.\n\n## Unwired-output discard rule\n\nThe general rule this issue makes use of, applicable to every\nbox:\n\n> **If an output value is produced but no wire carries it\n> downstream, the value is discarded.**\n\nA `write` box's done boolean is the most visible case — a user\nwho doesn't need a chain-after-write trigger leaves the output\nunwired and the runtime drops the value. The rule already holds\ninformally for every box; documenting it here (and in\n`docs/001-architecture.md`) makes it explicit.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Block on 317**: cross-language emit/write callbacks must be\n   in place. Without them this issue degrades to plain-text IO.\n2. **Schema** (`src/001-schema.lua`, `src/010-graph-loader.c`):\n   accept `read` and `write`; retire `data`.\n3. **Loader migration** (`src/003-loader.lua`): rewrite legacy\n   `data` boxes per the migration section.\n4. **Phase 2 executor** (`src/004-executor.lua`): handle `read`\n   (literal or file) and `write` directly. Cross-language\n   conversion uses the spec callbacks via the same path as\n   call-box value transport.\n5. **Phase 3 dispatch** (`src/012-dispatch.c`): same handling at\n   the dispatch layer. `read`'s fan-out loops through downstream\n   wires per spec; `write` looks up source-spec on its `value`\n   input.\n6. **Inspector** (`assets/js/004-inspector.js`): kind-specific\n   layout per \"Inspector behavior\" above. The inline-value field\n   for `read` is new; the port-hide-when-literal-value behavior\n   is new and needs a small render-side hook in `draw_box`.\n7. **Box rendering** (`assets/js/002-boxes.js`):\n   - Add `read: '#4caf7d'` and `write: '#d4762a'` to `KIND_COLOR`.\n   - Add `read`/`write` to the `KIND_HEADER` map from issue 236.\n   - Honor `hide_port` flag (or equivalent) on the path input\n     when the inline value is set on a `read` box.\n8. **Documentation**: update `docs/001-architecture.md` with the\n   new kinds, the unwired-output rule, and the language-aware\n   IO behavior. Update the dispatch-layer info.md.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Output port labels** for `read` and `write`: `contents` for\n  read, `done` for write — pick once, document, move on. Issue\n  236 already established the per-kind output-label table; add\n  these two rows.\n- **Static path on `write`**: should `write` also accept an\n  inline literal path on its `path` port (same way `read`\n  does)? Probably yes — the use case \"save to a fixed location\n  every time\" is common. Comes free if we apply the existing\n  port-literal-value mechanism.\n- **`read` with both literal and path set on disk** (a user who\n  edits the JSON by hand and sets both): validator rejects, or\n  literal-wins? Validator rejects — explicit error rather than\n  hidden precedence.\n- **Cross-language type fidelity** for the C spec: walking\n  arbitrary C structs is rabbit-hole territory (issue 317\n  tracks this). Until C's `native_to_json` handles structs,\n  C-source `write` boxes are limited to scalar values. Same\n  limitation issue 317 documents.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — kind validation, new shapes\n- `src/010-graph-loader.c` — C-side schema, migration\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — legacy `data` rewrite\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — phase 2 runtime handling\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — phase 3 dispatch primitives\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — kind-specific inspector layout\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — color, header, port-hide on literal\n- `langs/{lua,c,bash}/spec.c` — `native_to_json` / `json_to_native`\n  (issue 317 owns these)\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — kinds section, unwired-output rule\n- `issues/317-spec-json-bridge-for-data-boxes.md` — hard dependency\n- `issues/235-...completed/` — literal-replaces-port-name idea\n  extended to \"literal hides port entirely\" here\n- `issues/236-...completed/` — per-kind header/output-label map\n- `issues/completed/216-read-file-box.md` — Lua-side read superseded\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — phase 3 home for these\n- `issues/completed/109-data-files-persistent-and-ephemeral.md` —\n  `soramech-data` is a separate concern; not affected\n\n---\n\n## Historical proposals (superseded)\n\n### Revision 2 (single `data` kind, literal-or-file)\n\nProposed one unified source box: literal value typed in the\ninspector OR file at `path`. Plus a separate `write` sink.\nRejected because the source-and-sink-in-one-kind ambiguity\nanalysis (above, in \"Why two kinds\") flagged real footguns —\nthe `path`-input-without-`value` case silently reading from\na file the user meant to write to.\n\n### Revision 1 (`data` source + `file_write` sink)\n\nProposed a `data` kind (no inputs, just a `path` field; emits\nfile bytes) and a separate write-sink. Renamed in revision 2\nto `read` / `write` because verbs match what the boxes do\nbetter than `data` does. Both revisions kept the same source\n/ sink split.\n\nThe binary-data, atomic-write, JSON-parsing, and dispatch-layer\nhome questions all carry over unchanged through every\nrevision.\n",

Picking a kind from this dropdown\nswaps the box's input/output shape per the schemas above.\n\n## Migration\n\nLegacy `data` boxes (the cosmetic-only kind) get rewritten by\nthe loader. Two paths:\n\n- Boxes with a `ref` / `fn` (the call-equivalent shape they\n  carry today) → rewrite `kind` to `call`. Behavior identical\n  to current.\n- Boxes without a `ref` / `fn` (rare — would be invalid today)\n  → rewrite to `read` with no path; the validator then flags\n  them so the user notices and fills in a path or literal.\n\nThe `data` kind is retired entirely. The schema rejects it\nafter migration runs once.\n\n## Unwired-output discard rule\n\nThe general rule this issue makes use of, applicable to every\nbox:\n\n> **If an output value is produced but no wire carries it\n> downstream, the value is discarded.**\n\nA `write` box's done boolean is the most visible case — a user\nwho doesn't need a chain-after-write trigger leaves the output\nunwired and the runtime drops the value. The rule already holds\ninformally for every box; documenting it here (and in\n`docs/001-architecture.md`) makes it explicit.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Block on 317**: cross-language emit/write callbacks must be\n   in place. Without them this issue degrades to plain-text IO.\n2. **Schema** (`src/001-schema.lua`, `src/010-graph-loader.c`):\n   accept `read` and `write`; retire `data`.\n3. **Loader migration** (`src/003-loader.lua`): rewrite legacy\n   `data` boxes per the migration section.\n4. **Phase 2 executor** (`src/004-executor.lua`): handle `read`\n   (literal or file) and `write` directly. Cross-language\n   conversion uses the spec callbacks via the same path as\n   call-box value transport.\n5. **Phase 3 dispatch** (`src/012-dispatch.c`): same handling at\n   the dispatch layer. `read`'s fan-out loops through downstream\n   wires per spec; `write` looks up source-spec on its `value`\n   input.\n6. **Inspector** (`assets/js/004-inspector.js`): kind-specific\n   layout per \"Inspector behavior\" above. The inline-value field\n   for `read` is new; the port-hide-when-literal-value behavior\n   is new and needs a small render-side hook in `draw_box`.\n7. **Box rendering** (`assets/js/002-boxes.js`):\n   - Add `read: '#4caf7d'` and `write: '#d4762a'` to `KIND_COLOR`.\n   - Add `read`/`write` to the `KIND_HEADER` map from issue 236.\n   - Honor `hide_port` flag (or equivalent) on the path input\n     when the inline value is set on a `read` box.\n8. **Documentation**: update `docs/001-architecture.md` with the\n   new kinds, the unwired-output rule, and the language-aware\n   IO behavior. Update the dispatch-layer info.md.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Output port labels** for `read` and `write`: `contents` for\n  read, `done` for write — pick once, document, move on. Issue\n  236 already established the per-kind output-label table; add\n  these two rows.\n- **Static path on `write`**: should `write` also accept an\n  inline literal path on its `path` port (same way `read`\n  does)? Probably yes — the use case \"save to a fixed location\n  every time\" is common. Comes free if we apply the existing\n  port-literal-value mechanism.\n- **`read` with both literal and path set on disk** (a user who\n  edits the JSON by hand and sets both): validator rejects, or\n  literal-wins? Validator rejects — explicit error rather than\n  hidden precedence.\n- **Cross-language type fidelity** for the C spec: walking\n  arbitrary C structs is rabbit-hole territory (issue 317\n  tracks this). Until C's `native_to_json` handles structs,\n  C-source `write` boxes are limited to scalar values. Same\n  limitation issue 317 documents.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — kind validation, new shapes\n- `src/010-graph-loader.c` — C-side schema, migration\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — legacy `data` rewrite\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — phase 2 runtime handling\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — phase 3 dispatch primitives\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — kind-specific inspector layout\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — color, header, port-hide on literal\n- `langs/{lua,c,bash}/spec.c` — `native_to_json` / `json_to_native`\n  (issue 317 owns these)\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — kinds section, unwired-output rule\n- `issues/317-spec-json-bridge-for-data-boxes.md` — hard dependency\n- `issues/235-...completed/` — literal-replaces-port-name idea\n  extended to \"literal hides port entirely\" here\n- `issues/236-...completed/` — per-kind header/output-label map\n- `issues/completed/216-read-file-box.md` — Lua-side read superseded\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — phase 3 home for these\n- `issues/completed/109-data-files-persistent-and-ephemeral.md` —\n  `soramech-data` is a separate concern; not affected\n\n---\n\n## Historical proposals (superseded)\n\n### Revision 2 (single `data` kind, literal-or-file)\n\nProposed one unified source box: literal value typed in the\ninspector OR file at `path`. Plus a separate `write` sink.\nRejected because the source-and-sink-in-one-kind ambiguity\nanalysis (above, in \"Why two kinds\") flagged real footguns —\nthe `path`-input-without-`value` case silently reading from\na file the user meant to write to.\n\n### Revision 1 (`data` source + `file_write` sink)\n\nProposed a `data` kind (no inputs, just a `path` field; emits\nfile bytes) and a separate write-sink. Renamed in revision 2\nto `read` / `write` because verbs match what the boxes do\nbetter than `data` does. Both revisions kept the same source\n/ sink split.\n\nThe binary-data, atomic-write, JSON-parsing, and dispatch-layer\nhome questions all carry over unchanged through every\nrevision.\n",

          "content":"# 239 — Literal-bound input ports shrink to a nodule, port name moves to the left\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nPer issue 235 (complete), an input port whose literal value is\nset renders with the value in place of the port name. The dot\non the box's left edge stays full-size, and the port name\ndisappears from the canvas — only the value is visible. The\ninspector still owns the name, and the dot still works as a\nwire-grab target even though wiring into a port with a literal\nvalue would severs that literal on connect.\n\nWhat the user reading the map can see at a glance:\n\n```\n●  \"hello world\"\n```\n\nThe port's variable name (`text`, `prompt`, whatever it is in\nthe underlying function signature) is invisible on the canvas.\nA reader has to open the inspector to recover the binding.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA port with a literal value rendered in three pieces, in three\npositions, in this order left-to-right:\n\n```\ntext   ·   \"hello world\"\n```\n\n- **Port name** (`text`) — moved to the LEFT of the box's edge,\n  in the gutter just outside the box body. This is the\n  variable's identity, and 235's value-takes-over rendering\n  hid it. Pulling it out to the left puts the name back in\n  plain sight WITHOUT giving up the value display.\n- **Nodule** — a smaller, denser dot sitting where the regular\n  port dot would. About half the radius of a wired port's dot.\n  Visual marker only — it advertises \"this port is bound\" the\n  same way the regular dot advertises \"this port can be wired.\"\n  Color match its kind, same as the regular dot, so the eye\n  reads it as a port without confusion.\n- **Literal value** (`\"hello world\"`) — to the RIGHT of the\n  nodule, same position the regular port name occupies on a\n  wired port. Truncation rules from 235 still apply (24-char\n  limit with ellipsis, tooltip for the full value).\n\nA wired port stays exactly as it is today — full-size dot,\nname to its right, no left-of-box-edge label.\n\n### Wire-connect targeting disabled\n\nA literal-bound port is no longer a valid drag-target for\nwires. `Boxes.hit_test_port` excludes literal-bound input ports\nfrom its hit search, so:\n\n- The cursor over a nodule does NOT highlight the port for a\n  wire-grab.\n- The user cannot start drawing a wire from / to a literal-bound\n  port. To rebind, they clear the literal value in the inspector\n  first; the port then renders as a wirable dot again.\n\nToday, dropping a wire onto a port with a literal value silently\nclears the literal (per the existing inspector code, line ~656\nin `004-inspector.js`). That behavior was a defensible\ncompromise pre-239 because the value was the only visible\nstate — losing it to a wire was reversible by re-typing.\nPost-239 the user is explicitly indicating \"this is bound, no\nwires,\" so we honor that instead of dropping a value on accident.\n\n### Why this is better than the 235-only rendering\n\n- The user reading a map sees BOTH the variable identity and\n  the bound value, on one line, without inspector lookup.\n- The nodule is unambiguously \"not a wire target,\" so the user\n  doesn't waste a drag attempt only to learn the literal was\n  silently cleared.\n- The left-of-edge name uses canvas gutter space that is\n  currently empty, so the box body's horizontal budget is\n  unaffected.\n\n### Edge cases\n\n- **Multiple ports with literals**: each gets its own left-of-\n  edge name. Boxes with several literal-bound ports show a\n  cleanly-stacked column of names in the gutter.\n- **Variadic slot with a literal**: same rule as any other\n  port. The variadic group's auto-grow / hide-empty-trailing\n  rules from issue 217 are unaffected.\n- **Port name long enough to collide with the left-of-edge\n  gutter of an adjacent box**: clip with ellipsis at the box's\n  max gutter width (TBD constant; ~12 monospace chars at\n  10px gives ~72 world-px gutter, which is fine for typical\n  identifiers). Tooltip on hover for the full name, same as\n  235's value tooltip.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `assets/js/002-boxes.js`:\n   - Add a `port_is_literal_bound(box, i)` helper. Returns true\n     when the port has a value AND no incoming wire. (The same\n     three-state check `port_label_text` already does — pull it\n     into a shared helper.)\n   - In `draw_box`'s input-port loop: when literal-bound, draw\n     the nodule (half-radius, same fill/stroke style as a normal\n     dot) instead of the full dot; render the port name to the\n     LEFT of the dot position (textAlign right, with the box's\n     world x as the right edge); the value label drawing\n     continues unchanged (235 path).\n   - `hit_test_port`: skip ports that are literal-bound on\n     inputs. The output side is unaffected (outputs don't carry\n     literal values).\n2. `assets/js/006-wires.js::create_connection`: the\n   sever-literal-on-connect path in 004-inspector.js becomes\n   unreachable because the literal port can't be a drag target.\n   It can stay as a defensive guard in case some other code\n   path forces a connection.\n3. Tests: extend the 235 case set with two new cases:\n   - \"wire attached, literal present\" → still renders as wired\n     (wire wins, no nodule).\n   - \"literal only\" → renders nodule + left-name + right-value.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Nodule radius**: half (3px world) is a starting guess. Visual\n  weight will tell us if it should be smaller; refine after\n  shipping. Constant in 002-boxes.js so it's a one-line change.\n- **Gutter clip width**: 12 chars at 10px is a guess. Could be\n  expressed as a fraction of `BOX_W` to scale if BOX_W ever\n  changes. Probably not worth parameterizing today.\n- **Inspector indication of \"this port is literal-bound\"**: the\n  inspector already shows the value field; that's the only\n  binding state. No additional UI needed there — the canvas is\n  the place where the visual rule applies.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — `draw_box` input-port path,\n  `hit_test_port`, helpers\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — sever-on-connect guard\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — sever-on-set guard (still\n  fires when the user sets a literal through the inspector\n  while a wire is attached; the wire-into-literal direction is\n  the one this issue closes off)\n- `issues/completed/235-literal-value-replaces-port-name-on-canvas.md`\n  — the predecessor; the value-on-canvas rule this issue\n  retains, the dot-stays-the-same-size rule this issue\n  supersedes\n",

      "content":"-- Schema definitions and validators for SoraMech map files.\n-- Validates box files, meta.json, and drivers.json against the spec\n-- in docs/001-architecture.md. Used by both the runner and the server\n-- before any file is written to disk.\n\nlocal DIR = \"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\n\nlocal M = {}\n\n-- {{{ valid_kinds\nlocal valid_kinds = { call = true, data = true }\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ valid_branches\n-- null/nil means no comparator (single wire); the three strings are comparator outputs.\nlocal valid_branches = { lt = true, eq = true, gt = true }\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ err\nlocal function err(errors, msg)\n    errors[#errors + 1] = msg\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ validate_connection\nlocal function validate_connection(c, i, errors)\n    -- from_branch is nil (no comparator) or one of \"lt\"/\"eq\"/\"gt\"\n    if c.from_box == nil then\n        err(errors, \"connection[\" .. i .. \"] missing 'from_box'\")\n    end\n    if c.from_branch ~= nil and not valid_branches[c.from_branch] then\n        err(errors, \"connection[\" .. i .. \"] 'from_branch' must be nil, 'lt', 'eq', or 'gt'\")\n    end\n    if c.to_box == nil then\n        err(errors, \"connection[\" .. i .. \"] missing 'to_box'\")\n    end\n    if c.to_input == nil then\n        err(errors, \"connection[\" .. i .. \"] missing 'to_input'\")\n    end\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ validate_box\nfunction M.validate_box(box)\n    local errors = {}\n    if type(box) ~= \"table\" then\n        return { \"box must be a table\" }\n    end\n\n    if box.id == nil or type(box.id) ~= \"string\" then\n        err(errors, \"missing or non-string 'id'\")\n    end\n    if box.label == nil or type(box.label) ~= \"string\" then\n        err(errors, \"missing or non-string 'label'\")\n    end\n    if box.kind == nil or not valid_kinds[box.kind] then\n        err(errors, \"missing or invalid 'kind' (must be 'call' or 'data')\")\n    end\n\n    if box.kind == \"call\" or box.kind == \"data\" then\n        -- iterator boxes (issue 221) are a pure routing primitive: input\n        -- copies straight to a chosen output, no language function is\n        -- invoked. Such a box has no ref/fn — only `iterator_outputs`,\n        -- an ordered list of output slot names. Otherwise ref is required.\n        local is_iterator = box.iterator_outputs ~= nil\n        if not is_iterator then\n            if box.ref == nil or type(box.ref) ~= \"string\" then\n                err(errors, \"box missing 'ref'\")\n            end\n        end\n        if box.iterator_outputs ~= nil then\n            if type(box.iterator_outputs) ~= \"table\" then\n                err(errors, \"'iterator_outputs' must be an array\")\n            else\n                for i, name in ipairs(box.iterator_outputs) do\n                    if type(name) ~= \"string\" then\n                        err(errors, \"'iterator_outputs[\" .. i .. \"]' must be a string\")\n                    end\n                end\n            end\n        end\n        -- fn is optional for binary callers (shell scripts, binaries)\n        if box.inputs ~= nil and type(box.inputs) ~= \"table\" then\n            err(errors, \"'inputs' must be an array\")\n        end\n        -- variadic_inputs: optional list of base names; each name must\n        -- correspond to a series of inputs named \"<base>_<index>\" in\n        -- box.inputs (the editor maintains this; we only check the\n        -- shape here). See issue 217 part B.\n        if box.variadic_inputs ~= nil then\n            if type(box.variadic_inputs) ~= \"table\" then\n                err(errors, \"'variadic_inputs' must be an array\")\n            else\n                for i, name in ipairs(box.variadic_inputs) do\n                    if type(name) ~= \"string\" then\n                        err(errors, \"'variadic_inputs[\" .. i .. \"]' must be a string\")\n                    end\n                end\n            end\n        end\n        -- comparand: optional; if present it must be a string parseable as number at runtime\n        if box.comparand ~= nil and type(box.comparand) ~= \"string\" then\n            err(errors, \"'comparand' must be a string\")\n        end\n        -- has_output: optional; absence means \"true\" (default behavior).\n        -- false marks a sink box whose function has no return values\n        -- (issue 226); the runtime treats such boxes as terminal and the\n        -- editor hides the output port and inspector output section.\n        if box.has_output ~= nil and type(box.has_output) ~= \"boolean\" then\n            err(errors, \"'has_output' must be a boolean\")\n        end\n        if box.connections ~= nil then\n            for i, c in ipairs(box.connections) do\n                validate_connection(c, i, errors)\n            end\n        end\n    end\n\n    if box.ui ~= nil then\n        if type(box.ui) ~= \"table\" then\n            err(errors, \"'ui' must be a table\")\n        elseif box.ui.x == nil or box.ui.y == nil then\n            err(errors, \"'ui' must have 'x' and 'y' fields\")\n        end\n    end\n\n    return errors\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ validate_meta\nfunction M.validate_meta(meta)\n    local errors = {}\n    if type(meta) ~= \"table\" then\n        return { \"meta.json must be a table\" }\n    end\n    if meta.name == nil or type(meta.name) ~= \"string\" then\n        err(errors, \"meta.json missing 'name'\")\n    end\n    if meta.entry_box_id == nil or type(meta.entry_box_id) ~= \"string\" then\n        err(errors, \"meta.json missing 'entry_box_id'\")\n    end\n    return errors\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ validate_drivers\nfunction M.validate_drivers(drivers)\n    local errors = {}\n    if type(drivers) ~= \"table\" then\n        return { \"drivers.json must be a table\" }\n    end\n    for ext, path in pairs(drivers) do\n        if type(ext) ~= \"string\" or ext:sub(1, 1) ~= \".\" then\n            err(errors, \"driver key '\" .. tostring(ext) .. \"' must be a dot-prefixed extension\")\n        end\n        if type(path) ~= \"string\" then\n            err(errors, \"driver value for '\" .. ext .. \"' must be a string path\")\n        end\n    end\n    return errors\nend\n-- }}}\n\nreturn M\n",

Non-first slot — \"×\" removes that slot\n        const btn_style = 'background:none;border:1px solid #2a2f45;border-radius:3px;' +\n          'color:#6c72a0;cursor:pointer;font-family:monospace;font-size:9px;' +\n          'padding:1px 5px;line-height:1.4;';\n\n        if (!in_var_group) {\n          const var_btn = document.createElement('button');\n          var_btn.style.cssText = btn_style;\n          var_btn.textContent   = 'var';\n          var_btn.title         = 'mark this input as variadic (grows to N slots)';\n          var_btn.onclick       = () => make_variadic(p.name);\n          top_row.appendChild(var_btn);\n        } else if (pv.index === 0) {\n          const var_btn = document.createElement('button');\n          var_btn.style.cssText = btn_style + 'border-color:#4a9eff;color:#4a9eff;';\n          var_btn.textContent   = 'var ×';\n          var_btn.title         = 'collapse back to a single non-variadic input';\n          var_btn.onclick       = () => unmake_variadic(pv.base);\n          top_row.appendChild(var_btn);\n        } else {\n          const x_btn = document.createElement('button');\n          x_btn.style.cssText = btn_style;\n          x_btn.textContent   = '×';\n          x_btn.title         = 'remove this slot';\n          x_btn.onclick       = () => remove_variadic_slot(p.name);\n          top_row.appendChild(x_btn);\n        }\n\n        block.appendChild(top_row);\n\n        // Value input — full-width row below the name. Empty means\n        // \"no literal\" (wire supplies the value at runtime).\n        const val_inp = document.createElement('input');\n        val_inp.type        = 'text';\n        val_inp.value       = p.value !== undefined ? The check fails loud and points at the exact box +\n-- port instead.\n--\n-- `boxes` is a table mapping box-id → box record (the shape the\n-- editor cache and the phase 2 loader's graph use). Returns an\n-- array of error strings; empty array means OK.\nfunction M.check_input_bindings(boxes)\n    local errors = {}\n\n    -- precompute: for each (to_box, to_input) → true if a wire targets it.\n    -- Connections live on both endpoints (issue 228), so scanning every\n    -- box's connection list overcounts but doesn't miss anything.\n    local wired = {}\n    for _, box in pairs(boxes) do\n        for _, c in ipairs(box.connections or {}) do\n            if c.to_box and c.to_input then\n                wired[c.to_box .. \"\\0\" .. c.to_input] = true\n            end\n        end\n    end\n\n    -- stable per-box iteration for predictable error ordering\n    local ids = {}\n    for id, _ in pairs(boxes) do ids[#ids + 1] = id end\n    table.sort(ids)\n\n    for _, id in ipairs(ids) do\n        local box = boxes[id]\n        for _, p in ipairs(box.inputs or {}) do\n            local has_wire    = wired[id .. \"\\0\" .. p.name] == true\n            local has_literal = p.value ~= nil and p.value ~= \"\"\n            local is_optional = p.optional == true\n            if not (has_wire or has_literal or is_optional) then\n                err(errors, \"box '\" .. id .. \"': input '\" .. tostring(p.name) ..\n                    \"' has no wire, no literal, and is not optional\")\n            end\n        end\n    end\n\n    return errors\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ validate_meta",

running from any directory by finding libs relative to DIR\npackage.path = DIR .. \"/libs/?.lua;\" ..\n               DIR .. \"/src/?.lua;\" ..\n               package.path\n\nlocal json   = require(\"dkjson\")\nlocal schema = require(\"001-schema\")\n\n-- {{{ read_file\nlocal function read_file(path)\n    local f, ferr = io.open(path, \"r\")\n    if not f then return nil, ferr end\n    local contents = f:read(\"*a\")\n    f:close()\n    return contents\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ parse_json_file\nlocal function parse_json_file(path)\n    local raw, ferr = read_file(path)\n    if not raw then return nil, \"cannot open \" .. path .. \": \" .. ferr end\n    local obj, _, jerr = json.decode(raw)\n    if not obj then return nil, \"JSON error in \" .. path .. \": \" .. jerr end\n    return obj\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ load_boxes\nlocal function load_boxes(map_dir)\n    -- returns table of {id -> box_table} and a list of errors\n    local boxes = {}\n    local errors = {}\n    local boxes_dir = map_dir .. \"/boxes\"\n\n    local handle = io.popen(\"ls \" .. boxes_dir .. \"/*.json 2>/dev/null\")\n    if not handle then\n        return boxes, { \"cannot list \" .. boxes_dir }\n    end\n    local listing = handle:read(\"*a\")\n    handle:close()\n\n    for path in listing:gmatch(\"[^\\n]+\") do\n        local box, berr = parse_json_file(path)\n        if not box then\n            errors[#errors + 1] = berr\n        else\n            local box_errors = schema.validate_box(box)\n            if #box_errors > 0 then\n                for _, e in ipairs(box_errors) do\n                    errors[#errors + 1] = path .. \": \" .. e\n                end\n            else\n                boxes[box.id] = box\n            end\n        end\n    end\n\n    return boxes, errors\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ check_connections\nlocal function check_connections(boxes, errors)\n    -- each connection is stored in BOTH endpoint box files as the same 4-field record.\n    -- we only process connections where from_box == this box's id (outgoing connections).\n    -- incoming reciprocal records (from_box != id) are skipped here; they are validated\n    -- implicitly when we process the source box.\n    for id, box in pairs(boxes) do\n        local conns = box.connections or {}\n        for _, c in ipairs(conns) do\n            if c.from_box ~= id then\n                -- this is the reciprocal copy stored for reference; skip\n                goto next_conn\n            end\n\n            local target = boxes[c.to_box]\n            if target == nil then\n                errors[#errors + 1] = \"box '\" .. id .. \"': connection to unknown box '\" ..\n                    tostring(c.to_box) .. \"'\"\n            else\n                -- find exact match in target: all four fields must agree\n                local found = false\n                for _, tc in ipairs(target.connections or {}) do\n                    if tc.from_box    == c.from_box   and\n                       tc.from_output == c.from_output and\n                       tc.to_box      == c.to_box      and\n                       tc.to_input    == c.to_input    then\n                        found = true\n                        break\n                    end\n                end\n                if not found then\n                    errors[#errors + 1] = \"box '\" .. id .. \"': connection \" ..\n                        c.from_box .. \".\" .. c.from_output ..\n                        \" -> \" .. c.to_box .. \".\" .. c.to_input ..\n                        \" not found in target box file (both ends must store the same record)\"\n                end\n            end\n\n            ::next_conn::\n        end\n    end\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ check_branch_else\nlocal function check_branch_else(boxes, errors)\n    -- branch boxes must have an \"else\" port (enforced by schema, re-checked here\n    -- for clarity), and numeric/string-predicate branch boxes must wire \"else\"\n    for id, box in pairs(boxes) do\n        if box.kind ~= \"branch\" then goto continue end\n\n        local has_else_port = false\n        local has_else_wire = false\n        for _, p in ipairs(box.ports or {}) do\n            if p.name == \"else\" then\n                has_else_port = true\n            end\n        end\n        for _, c in ipairs(box.connections or {}) do\n            if c.from_port == \"else\" then\n                has_else_wire = true\n            end\n        end\n\n        if not has_else_port then\n            errors[#errors + 1] = \"branch box '\" .. id .. \"' missing 'else' port\"\n        end\n\n        -- if else is unwired, the box must have retry_vary upstream to be valid;\n        -- we cannot check retry_vary here without traversing upstream, so we emit\n        -- a warning rather than a hard error — the runner will enforce at execute time\n        if has_else_port and not has_else_wire then\n            errors[#errors + 1] = \"branch box '\" .. id ..\n                \"': 'else' port is unwired (valid only for LLM retry; runner will \" ..\n                \"require upstream box to have retry_vary defined)\"\n        end\n\n        ::continue::\n    end\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ validate_map\nlocal function validate_map(map_dir)\n    local errors = {}\n\n    -- meta.json\n    local meta, merr = parse_json_file(map_dir .. errors[#errors + 1] = \"meta.json: \" .. e\n        end\n    end\n\n    -- drivers.json\n    local drivers, derr = parse_json_file(map_dir .. \"/drivers.json\")\n    if not drivers then\n        errors[#errors + 1] = derr\n    else\n        local driver_errors = schema.validate_drivers(drivers)\n        for _, e in ipairs(driver_errors) do\n            errors[#errors + 1] = \"drivers.json: \" .. e\n        end\n    end\n\n    -- boxes\n    local boxes, box_errors = load_boxes(map_dir)\n    for _, e in ipairs(box_errors) do\n        errors[#errors + 1] = e\n    end\n\n    -- cross-box \"' does not match any box file\"\n            end\n        end\n    end\n\n    return errors\nend\n-- }}}\n\n-- {{{ main\nlocal function main(args)\n    local map_dir = args[1]\n    if map_dir == nil then\n        io.stderr:write(\"usage: luajit 002-validate-map.lua <map-dir>\\n\")\n        os.exit(1)\n    end\n\n    local errors = validate_map(map_dir)\n\n    if #errors == 0 then\n         },
        "id":"toolu_01C3MWuUnfCXGAT6BZzqmiG9",
        "type":"tool_use",
        "input":{
          "old_string":"  // {{{ compile_map\n  // Placeholder for the phase 3 compile pipeline (issue 219). The button\n  // exists so the toolbar layout is settled before the backend is wired\n  // in. When implemented, this will POST to /maps/<name>/compile and\n  // produce a self-contained `compiled/` directory in the map:\n  //   compiled/pool-runner   — the C pool runner binary\n  //   compiled/src/          — copy of every source file the map uses\n  //   compiled/bin/          — per-box compiled .so files (C boxes)\n  //   compiled/langs/        — language spec .so files needed\n  //   compiled/manifest.json — every box, its language, its artifact path\n  function compile_map() {\n    console.log('compile clicked');\n    status_msg('compile is not wired up yet — see issue 219');\n  }\n  // }}}",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"  // {{{ check_input_bindings\n  // Issue 230: every input port must be wired, littered, or flagged\n  // optional. Mirrors src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings — the\n  // server-side validator runs the same logic when validate-map is\n  // invoked from the CLI. Returns [] on success, an array of\n  // human-readable error strings otherwise.\n  function check_input_bindings() {\n    // precompute: which (to_box, to_input) pairs have an incoming wire\n    const wired = new Set();\n    for (const id in Boxes.boxes) {\n      const conns = Boxes.boxes[id].connections || [];\n      for (const c of conns) {\n        if (c.to_box && c.to_input) {\n          wired.add(c.to_box + '\\0' + c.to_input);\n        }\n      }\n    }\n\n    const errors = [];\n    const ids = Object.keys(Boxes.boxes).sort();\n    for (const id of ids) {\n      const box = Boxes.boxes[id];\n      for (const p of (box.inputs || [])) {\n        const has_wire    = wired.has(id + '\\0' + p.name);\n        const has_literal = p.value !== undefined && p.value !== null && p.value !== '';\n        const is_optional = p.optional === true;\n        if (!(has_wire || has_literal || is_optional)) {\n          errors.push(\"box '\" + id + \"': input '\" + p.name +\n            \"' has no wire, no literal, and is not optional\");\n        }\n      }\n    }\n    return errors;\n  }\n  // }}}\n\n  // {{{ compile_map\n  // Pre-flight for the phase 3 compile pipeline (issue 219, folded\n  // into 309). The actual compile is the other dev's territory; here\n  // we run the issue-230 input-binding check so the user gets a hard\n  // stop on missing wires before whatever compile pipeline eventually\n  // lands. Errors print to the console (full list) and the first one\n  // surfaces in the status bar.\n  function compile_map() {\n    const errors = check_input_bindings();\n    if (errors.length > 0) {\n      console.warn('compile blocked — input-binding errors:');\n      errors.forEach(e => console.warn('  ' + e));\n      const summary = errors.length === 1\n        ? errors[0]\n        : errors.length + ' input-binding errors (see console for the full list); first: ' + errors[0];\n      status_msg(summary, 'error');\n      return;\n    }\n    console.log('compile clicked — input bindings OK');\n    status_msg('input bindings OK — compile pipeline not wired up yet (see issue 219)');\n  }\n  // }}}",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/assets/js/005-app.js"
        }
      }],

    "id":"msg_01Wv4BGevX7LhRpceeVXMcb6",

        "type":"text",
        "text":"The `var` button has three states depending on which port you click it on:\n\n| port state | button | what clicking does |\n|---|---|---|\n| plain port (e.g. `text`) | `var` | Convert to a variadic group with one slot. The port is renamed `text_0`. |\n| first slot of a group (`text_0`) | `var ×` | Collapse the whole group back to a single port. Drops slots 1+, renames `text_0` → `text`. |\n| any later slot (`text_1`, `text_2`, …) | `×` | Remove just that slot. Higher slots rename down (`text_2` → `text_1`, etc). |\n\nThe two automatic behaviors layered on top:\n\n- **Auto-grow**: when you wire to the *last* slot of a variadic group, the editor immediately adds a new empty `text_N+1` slot. Same thing fires when you set a literal value on the last slot. So you never have to click `var` more than once — just keep wiring and the slots appear under you.\n- **No auto-shrink**: disconnecting a wire or clearing a literal doesn't remove the slot. The `×` button is the only way to delete a slot. This was a deliberate call from 217 so transient editing (unplug, replug) doesn't lose your structure.\n\nOn the function side, what makes this work is the language's native variadic syntax — `function M.concat(sep, ...)` in Lua, `\"$@\"` after a shift in Bash, `argc` / `argv` for a C box. The editor's `text_0`, `text_1`, `text_2`, … map onto the positional args after any fixed-name inputs (`sep` in the concat example stays as a regular, non-variadic input).\n\nA common use case: `libs/text.lua`'s `M.concat(sep, ...)` — `sep` is plain, `text` you click `var` on, and now you can keep wiring `text_0`, `text_1`, `text_2` from whichever sources you want them joined from. The whole row collapses to one literal join at runtime."
      }],
