        "type":"text",
        "text":"It does the silent-wrong thing today, and there's no guardrail.\n\nWhat actually happens at runtime:\n\n- Lua / Bash silently swallow the extra args. If your function is `function M.upper(text)` and the editor sends three args from `text_0`, `text_1`, `text_2`, Lua treats `text = text_0_val` and drops the rest. Same shape with Bash — extra `$N` arguments exist but the function body never references them.\n- C is worse — if the wrapper's `n_inputs` doesn't match the declared parameter count, you'd typically get an error from the wrapper, but the exact behavior depends on what 307's wrapper convention ends up being.\n\nSo the user wires up what looks like a five-input concat, three slots silently never reach the function, and the only signal is \"the output is wrong.\" That's the same silent-error class 230 just fixed for missing-required-inputs, but in the other direction.\n\n**The editor doesn't check.** Today the `var` toggle is purely editor-side state — it changes the box JSON shape (slot names, the `variadic_inputs` list) and the runtime assembles positional args from it, but nothing cross-references the underlying source function. The file browser parses the source on initial pick, but a later `var` click never re-asks the source whether it actually accepts varargs.\n\n**There's a placeholder for the right answer** in 217's `## Future development ideas` section — \"Language-spec-driven variadic detection.\" Each language spec would expose `parse_function_signature` or similar that tells the editor \"this function is variadic on parameter N\" — and the editor would refuse to toggle `var` on a non-variadic parameter (or auto-toggle it on a variadic one). 231 (move parsers into `langs/<name>/parser.js`) is the natural prerequisite — once the per-language parser knows about variadicness, the editor just asks.\n\nWant me to open a small ticket for \"reject `var` toggle on non-variadic parameters\" as a follow-up? Or fold it into 231's scope (since 231 is already moving the parsers around)?"
      }],

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Fair — every ticket is part of the system's permanent history, none are throwaway.\n\nLet me answer the four questions in order.\n\n**Why is the button in the editor instead of the spec?** Mostly history. 217 shipped before the phase-3 language-spec system was anything more than a stub. Per-language knowledge had to live somewhere, and \"somewhere\" at the time was the editor's JavaScript. Specifically: `assets/js/007-filebrowser.js` carries hard-coded `parse_lua` and `parse_bash` functions that walk function signatures and pull out parameter names. The `var` toggle is the editor's hedge against not actually knowing whether a parameter is variadic — it lets the user *assert* \"this one is\" instead of detecting it. Phase 3 (issues 301–317) is the build-out of the real spec system. Once that's there, the editor stops needing to ask the user.\n\n**What does the right answer look like once a user is defining their own language spec?** Per the issue 303 / 307 / 308 contract, a language spec is a directory like `langs/<name>/` containing:\n\n- `spec.c` — the runtime side. Defines a `lang_spec_t` struct (issue 303) with callbacks for `init`, `invoke`, `teardown`, etc. The runtime asks the spec to invoke a function with N arguments.\n- `Makefile` — builds `spec.c` into a `.so` the pool loads at startup.\n- `parser.js` *(this part is issue 231)* — the editor-side. An ES module exporting:\n\n  ```js\n  export function parse_function_signature(source_text, fn_name) {\n    return {\n      name: '…',\n      inputs: ['sep', 'text'],\n      variadic_inputs: ['text'],     // names whose slots can be many\n      output: 'result',\n    };\n  }\n  ```\n\nThat's the whole contract on the editor side. When the user picks a function in the file browser, the editor calls this parser. The result tells the inspector \"here are the inputs, and *this one* is variadic.\" From there the variadic UI runs by itself — the `var` button is no longer a *toggle* the user has to set; it's a *fact* the editor already knows. For a non-variadic param the button is either hidden, disabled, or simply absent. For a variadic param the slots auto-grow without ever asking.\n\nFor a user adding their own language (Python, say): they write `langs/python/spec.c` for the runtime invocation, and `langs/python/parser.js` for the editor surface. The parser detects `*args` / `**kwargs` and reports the right `variadic_inputs`. No editor changes. No JavaScript-side patches in `007-filebrowser.js`. The whole language is one drop-in directory.\n\n**Why isn't this part of 217?** 217 is complete and committed. Adding to its scope means re-opening it, which the project's immutability rule for completed tickets pushes against. The work also doesn't actually belong in 217's scope as 217 was framed — 217's *delivered* the variadic UI mechanic and was explicit that detection-from-source was deferred to \"language-spec-driven variadic detection\" as a future idea. That future is now 231's territory.\n\n**What is 231?** \"Move per-language signature parsers out of the file browser into `langs/<name>/parser.js`.\" Currently the editor's file browser has `parse_lua` and `parse_bash` hard-coded inside it — same way the variadic button is hard-coded as a manual toggle. 231 moves both pieces of per-language knowledge into the language's own directory, where they belong. The mechanical change is: cut `parse_lua` out of `007-filebrowser.js`, paste into `langs/lua/parser.js` as an ES module, change the file browser to dynamically import whichever parser matches the file extension. Once that lands:\n\n- Adding a new language is one new directory.\n- The parser's return value gets to grow new fields (`variadic_inputs`, `optional_inputs`, `output_type`, …) and the editor consumes them generically.\n- The variadic-not-actually-variadic question collapses into \"look at the spec, see if the param is in `variadic_inputs`, render accordingly.\"\n\nSo the answer to your earlier question isn't \"small ticket\" or \"fold into 231.\" It's: **231 is the prerequisite.** Once 231 lands, the variadic-detection behavior falls out of it almost for free — the parsers already produce a `variadic_inputs` list, the editor just stops trusting the user to know better and trusts the parser instead. That's worth a paragraph inside 231 explicitly, not a separate ticket.\n\nWant me to expand 231's spec to call out the variadic-correctness consequence and the corresponding inspector change?"
      }],

The init barrier (issue 301) calls init()\n * for every spec on every worker before unblocking task dispatch;\n * the dispatch action (issue 304) calls invoke() per task; the\n * compile-button pipeline (issue 309) calls compile() per source\n * file for languages whose compile pointer is non-NULL.\n *\n * Errors: a nonzero return from any callback is fatal. The dispatch\n * layer prints the error context and aborts. There is no recovery,\n * no retry, no per-task failed state. This is intentional.\n *\n * Issue 312 extends this contract with optional fast-path\n * callbacks: `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` are specialised\n * variants the dispatch layer prefers when wire classification\n * says they apply; `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` are\n * bridges used at language boundaries. Specs that don't set them\n * fall back to `invoke` for every call.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H\n#define SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H\n\n#include <stddef.h>\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Shared signatures */\n/* Invoke signature — shared by `invoke`, `invoke_native`, and\n * `invoke_json`. The dispatch layer picks which one to call based\n * on the wire-format classification in issue 312. */\ntypedef int (*lang_invoke_fn)(void *handle,\n                              const char *file_path,\n                              const char *fn_name,\n                              const void **input_data,\n                              const int   *input_sizes,\n                              int          n_inputs,\n                              void        *out_buf,\n                              int          out_buf_capacity,\n                              int         *out_size);\n\n/* Wire-format bridge: convert one direction of native ↔ JSON.\n * Used when a value crosses a language boundary. Spec sets one\n * or both; if NULL, the dispatch layer treats native and JSON as\n * identical byte streams (the current uniform-byte default). */\ntypedef int (*lang_bridge_fn)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                              void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ lang_spec_t */\ntypedef struct lang_spec {\n    const char *name;       /* \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ... */\n    const char *file_ext;   /* \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\"        */\n\n    /* init: once per worker thread at pool startup. Returns an\n     * opaque handle stored in the worker context; the dispatch\n     * layer passes this handle back to invoke() for every call. */\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n\n    /* teardown: once per worker at pool shutdown. Frees the handle\n     * and any per-worker resources (e.g. lua_State, dlopen caches,\n     * persistent socket connections). */\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n\n    /* compile: optional. Called once per source file at map-load\n     * (or at editor compile-button time). For languages that don't\n     * compile (Lua, Bash), leave this NULL. For C, it runs\n     * gcc -shared -fPIC -o out_path src_path. Returns 0 on\n     * success, nonzero on failure. */\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n\n    /* invoke: per box call. Inputs are arrays of (bytes, size) pairs,\n     * already read from slots by the dispatch layer. Returns the\n     * function's output by writing to out_buf and setting *out_size.\n     * Returns 0 on success, nonzero (fatal) on error.\n     *\n     * This is the canonical entry point; every spec implements it.\n     * The dispatch layer falls back to it when the specialised\n     * paths below are not set. */\n    lang_invoke_fn invoke;\n\n    /* invoke_native — optional fast path used when every wire\n     * adjacent to this box (input and output) stays inside this\n     * spec's language. Bytes on the wire are this language's\n     * native serialisation (Lua tables via msgpack, C struct\n     * memcpy, etc.) and the encode/decode round trip is skipped.\n     * NULL means the spec hasn't specialised; dispatch falls\n     * back to `invoke`. Issue 312. */\n    lang_invoke_fn invoke_native;\n\n    /* invoke_json — optional universal-interop path. Bytes on the\n     * wire are JSON. NULL means the spec hasn't specialised;\n     * dispatch falls back to `invoke`. Issue 312. */\n    lang_invoke_fn invoke_json;\n\n    /* Bridges between native and JSON wire forms. Used when a\n     * value crosses a language boundary — the producer writes\n     * native, the dispatch layer converts via the producer's\n     * native_to_json, hands the JSON bytes to the consumer's\n     * json_to_native. NULL means the spec hasn't specialised;\n     * dispatch treats native and JSON as identical bytes. Issue\n     * 312. */\n    lang_bridge_fn native_to_json;\n    lang_bridge_fn json_to_native;\n} lang_spec_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\n}\n#endif\n\n#endif /* SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H */\n",

The dispatch layer (issue 304) looks the\n * spec up at runtime to invoke a box's function.\n *\n * Lifetime: created at process startup, alive for the run, freed\n * at shutdown. dlclose() is called on every handle in destroy.\n *\n * Errors: spec_registry_load returns NULL and sets *err on failure\n * (cannot open langs_dir, dlopen failure, missing required symbol).\n * The caller frees *err.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_SPEC_REGISTRY_H\n#define SORAMECH_SPEC_REGISTRY_H\n\n#include \"lang-spec.h\"\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\ntypedef struct spec_registry spec_registry_t;\n\n/* Open every langs_dir/<name>/spec.so and read its\n * soramech_lang_spec symbol. Returns NULL on failure with *err set. */\nspec_registry_t *spec_registry_load(const char *langs_dir, char **err);\n\n/* dlclose every handle, free the registry. Safe on NULL. */\nvoid             spec_registry_destroy(spec_registry_t *r);\n\nint              spec_registry_size(const spec_registry_t *r);\n\n---\n/* langs/lua/spec.c — Lua language spec for SoraMech.\n *\n * Per-worker handle is a `lua_State` with the standard libraries\n * opened. Invocation convention: the box's source file is expected\n * to return a Lua table (`return M` at the bottom), and the\n * fn_name is a key into that table. Inputs arrive as byte arrays;\n * each one is pushed as a Lua string. The function's single return\n * value is converted to a string (via tostring semantics) and\n * memcpy'd into the caller's output buffer.\n *\n * Designed in issue 306. Implementation choices that matter:\n *\n *  - One lua_State per worker thread. lua_State is not\n *    thread-safe, but per-thread requires no locking.\n *  - The state's stack is rewound to its baseline depth at every\n *    invoke entry/exit so cross-call leaks don't accumulate.\n *  - File caching (luaL_loadfile once, replayed via lua_call) is\n *    deferred — this iteration loads the chunk on every invoke.\n *    Lands as a follow-on once profiling justifies it.\n *  - The chunk's side effects run on every invoke too (since\n *    we re-load and re-execute). Box source files should be pure\n *    \"return M\" modules for now.\n */\n\n#include \"lang-spec.h\"\n\n#include <lua.h>\n#include <lauxlib.h>\n#include <lualib.h>",

{

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Here's how it works, walking from outside in.\n\n**The contract is one C struct.** `langs/lang-spec.h` declares `lang_spec_t` — a struct of function pointers. A language spec is \"an instance of this struct, compiled into a `.so`, dropped at `langs/<name>/spec.so`.\" That's the whole interface. Anyone adding a language fills the struct out and ships the directory.\n\nThe fields in order of when they fire:\n\n```\ninit(worker_idx)        — at pool startup, once per worker thread.\n                           Returns an opaque handle the spec wants\n                           to carry around (Lua's lua_State, C's\n                           dlopen cache, Bash's persistent socket).\ncompile(src, out)       — optional. For languages that need a build\n                           step, called once per source file. C\n                           runs gcc -shared -fPIC. Lua and Bash\n                           leave this NULL.\ninvoke(handle, file, fn,\n       inputs, sizes, n,\n       out, cap, *out_size)\n                        — per box call. The runtime hands you bytes\n                           in, you write bytes out.\nteardown(handle)        — at pool shutdown, per worker.\n```\n\nPlus a few fast-path / bridge callbacks from 312 (`invoke_native`, `invoke_json`, `native_to_json`, `json_to_native`) that are optional — leave them NULL and dispatch falls back to the canonical `invoke`.\n\n**Discovery happens at startup.** `src/011-spec-registry.c` scans `langs/*/`, `dlopen`s each `spec.so`, reads the exported `soramech_lang_spec` symbol (the struct), and builds a name-and-extension-keyed lookup. The pool runner consults that registry per-worker to call `init`. The dispatch layer consults it per-task to call `invoke`.\n\n**How \"what you define\" turns into the call — today.** This is the part the existing implementation does the *least* automatic glue for. Three pieces:\n\n1. **The spec author writes plain C.** No glue generation. They write `static int my_invoke(...)` and assign it to `.invoke = my_invoke` in the exported struct. Same for `init`, `teardown`, etc. The \"spec\" *is* the hand-written C file.\n\n2. **The box author follows a per-language convention.** This is where you'd expect glue and where there mostly isn't any yet:\n   - **Lua box**: write a file that does `local M = {}; function M.foo(a, b) ... end; return M`. The Lua spec's invoke pushes each input as a Lua string, calls `M[fn_name](...)`, and writes the return value back out. The convention is \"return a table.\"\n   - **C box**: write a function with this *fixed signature*:\n     ```c\n     int my_fn(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n               void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size);\n     ```\n     The signature matches the spec's `invoke` shape minus the per-worker handle. Compile-time, the spec's `compile` runs gcc on the file; invoke-time, it dlsyms the symbol and calls it. **No wrapper generation today** — every C box reads its bytes by hand.\n   - **Bash box**: a function `my_fn() { ... }` in a `.sh`. The Bash spec's invoke runs the function via a persistent socketpair (issue 308) and reads stdout.\n\n3. **The glue is the `invoke` callback itself.** That callback's body is the user-facing translation layer between \"bytes on a wire\" and \"a call into the language.\" Each language's spec.c hand-codes it. For Lua: push, call, tostring, copy. For C: dlsym, call function pointer, return. For Bash: serialize, send over socket, read.\n\n**Where \"generated glue\" *will* matter — the typed wrapper from 307.** This is the piece that doesn't exist yet but is the natural next move. The C spec's comment calls it out (langs/c/spec.c lines 16–19): \"does not generate per-box wrappers from declared signatures (issue 307's optional advanced mode) — every C box uses the fixed signature above.\" The vision is:\n\n- The user writes `int my_add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }` — a plain C function with declared types.\n- A build step generates a wrapper file: `int my_add_wrapper(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n, void *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size) { int a = *(int*)inputs[0]; int b = *(int*)inputs[1]; int r = my_add(a, b); *(int*)out_buf = r; *out_size = sizeof(int); return 0; }`.\n- The user never sees the wrapper.\n\nThat wrapper file is the only place \"glue\" gets *generated* in the design as drafted. Everywhere else, the glue is hand-written inside the spec's `invoke`. And the wrapper-generation step itself is also hand-written in the C spec — the spec's `compile` callback would emit the wrapper from a signature it parsed from the source.\n\n**Where 217's variadic-detection fits.** Two layers, neither of which involves code generation:\n\n- **Editor side (issue 231)**: `langs/<name>/parser.js` exposes `parse_function_signature(source, fn_name)` returning `{inputs, variadic_inputs, ...}`. The editor's file browser and inspector consume it. This is pure JavaScript ES-module per language; no C, no runtime, no glue.\n- **Runtime side (already works)**: the spec's `invoke` receives `n_inputs` and `inputs[]` of whatever length the dispatch layer assembled. For Lua's `function M.foo(sep, ...)`, the spec pushes all N as Lua values and the `...` collects the tail naturally. For Bash, `\"$@\"` does the same. For C with the fixed-signature convention, `inputs[]` is just an N-element array — the user's box function reads as many as it cares about.\n\nSo **adding a new language is one directory:**\n\n```\nlangs/python/\n  spec.c          ← lang_spec_t with init/invoke/teardown for Python\n  Makefile        ← builds spec.c into spec.so against libpython\n  parser.js       ← parses def fn(*args): … and tells the editor\n```\n\nThe runtime sees the new `spec.so` at startup and registers it. The editor sees the new `parser.js` and uses it for `.py` files. The user never edits the editor or the dispatch layer.\n\nFor the variadic-correctness question: it's purely editor-side. When 217 is reopened, the work is \"after 231 lands, parser.js's `parse_function_signature` already produces `variadic_inputs`; the inspector consumes it and renders `var` differently for variadic-by-the-language vs not.\" Zero runtime change.\n\nDoes that map cleanly onto what you wanted to understand? If a specific layer is still murky I can drill in."

    "originalFile":"# 230 — Required inputs, the optional flag, and no-null-from-missing\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA box's input port can be left without a wire and without a literal\nvalue. The user had a wiring intent,\nforgot to plug something in, and the runtime quietly papered over\nthe mistake.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEvery input port is in one of three states by **compile time**:\n\n1. A wire is connected to it.\n2. A literal value is set on it.\n3. It carries `optional: true` on the port record.\n\n**Compile fails** when any port is in none of those states. The\nerror is precise: which box, which port. The Compile button (issue\n222) is the natural enforcement point, with the same check\nduplicating in the phase 3 graph loader (issue 305).\n\n### \"Optional\" is not \"null\"\n\n`optional: true` says \"this argument doesn't have to be passed.\" It\ndoes not mean \"pass null.\" At the spec boundary, an optional\nunwired un-littered port produces a shorter arg list — the language\nsees fewer arguments, not a null argument. Each language handles\nthat natively:\n\n- **Lua**: omitted args are `nil`. That's a language convention,\n  not a wire-level value. Inside the Lua function, `arg or default`\n  works.\n- **Bash**: a positional arg that wasn't passed is unset.\n  `${arg:-default}` provides a default.\n- **C**: the spec's compile callback (issue 307) generates a wrapper\n  that reads `n_inputs` and only forwards the args that are present.\n\n### Null as an explicit value (allowed)\n\nIf the user needs to pass null because some downstream library\nexpects it, they can — by typing the literal `null` into the value\nfield. That's a string on the wire encoded as JSON null. Each spec\nmaps it to its language's native null on the way in:\n\n| JSON value  | Lua    | Bash       | C       |\n|-------------|--------|------------|---------|\n| `null`      | nil    | empty `\"\"` | `NULL`  |\n| `42`        | 42     | `\"42\"`     | 42      |\n| `\"foo\"`     | `foo`  | `foo`      | `\"foo\"` |\n| `true`      | true   | `\"true\"`   | `1`     |\n\nThe crucial distinction: **explicit null arrives through the\nfunction call as a real argument**; **optional-and-absent does not\narrive at all**. Bash empty-string-vs-unset disappears in the\noptional path because the arg position simply isn't passed.\n\n### Schema\n\nAdd `optional` as an optional boolean on input port records:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"name\": \"config_path\",\n  \"type\": \"string\",\n  \"optional\": true\n}\n```\n\nAbsence means `false`. No migration; existing maps work unchanged.\n\n## Compile-time check\n\nThe check walks every box, every input. For each:\n- If the port has `value` set (literal): pass.\n- If any connection has `to_box === box.id && to_input === port.name`:\n  pass.\n- If `port.optional === true`: pass.\n- Otherwise: error, with a precise message:\n  `\"box <id>: input '<port>' has no wire, no literal, and is not optional\"`\n\nThe check runs:\n- **Editor** — on Compile button click (issue 222 → 309). Errors\n  surface in the editor without writing the compiled output.\n- **Loader** — at run time (phase 3 issue 305). Errors abort the\n  run. Belt and suspenders: the editor catches it but a hand-edited\n  map JSON can still trip the loader check.\n\n## Spec API for \"is this arg present?\"\n\nThe spec doesn't need to ask. The dispatch layer assembles\n`input_data[]` and `input_sizes[]` from the slots that actually\nhave values. An optional port that's absent isn't in those arrays;\n`n_inputs` is shorter by one. The spec invokes the language with\nthe args it received. The language's native call convention does\nthe rest.\n\nFor C specifically, the compile-callback-generated wrapper takes\n`int n_inputs` and a count-prefixed array. The wrapper picks the\nfirst M args that match its declared parameters and forwards them;\ntrailing optionals get omitted from the call (or filled with C's\nzero-valued types, depending on the wrapper convention). This is\nissue 307's territory.\n\n## Inspector UI\n\nA small per-port flag in the inspector's port block:\n\n```\n[name] [var] [opt]\n[ value ........... ]\n```\n\n`opt` toggles `port.optional` on the port record. Visual: same\nsmall button as `var` but distinct color.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Whether to allow optional + literal**: yes. A literal is an\n  explicit value; the optional flag is irrelevant when the value\n  is set. The compile check just needs all three signals\n  available; literal wins over optional.\n- **What syntax means \"explicit null literal\"**: lean toward\n  literally typing `null` (case-insensitive) in the value field.\n  An ambiguity arises when the user actually wants the string\n  `\"null\"` — escape it as `\"null\"` (with quotes) which the value\n  parser interprets as a string literal. Worth nailing down before\n  shipping.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — accept `optional` field\n- `src/003-loader.lua` (phase 2) — compile-time check\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — `opt` toggle in port block\n- `assets/js/005-app.js` — Compile button hooks check before\n  compile\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — compile/package step calls the\n  check\n- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — phase 3 check at load time\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — `invoke`'s n_inputs\n  reflects what was actually passed\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — wrapper handles short-arg case\n- `issues/308-bash-language-spec.md` — null vs unset distinction\n  evaporates in the optional path\n",

          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"# 217 — Concat box with per-input variadic ports and auto-grow/shrink\n\n## Status\ncomplete (Part A, B); reopened for Part C — spec-driven variadic\ncorrectness, blocked on issue 231\n\n## Part C — reject `var` on a non-variadic parameter\n\nThe editor's `var` toggle is a user-asserted flag today. If the\nunderlying function signature doesn't accept varargs, the editor\nstill lets the user mark a parameter variadic; at runtime the\nextra positional args are silently swallowed (Lua / Bash drop\nunreferenced trailing args; C's fixed-signature wrapper either\nignores them or errors depending on how `n_inputs` is consumed).\n\nThis is the silent-error class — a sibling of the missing-input\ncase issue 230 closed off. The editor knows enough about the\nfunction (the file browser parsed its signature when the user\npicked it) to refuse the `var` toggle on a non-variadic\nparameter, but the parser today lives inside the editor's\nJavaScript and hard-codes the per-language rules — so the\ndetection's natural home is wherever the per-language parser\nmoves to next. That destination is issue 231 (move signature\nparsers into `langs/<name>/parser.js`).\n\n### Behavior after 231 lands\n\nThe `parse_function_signature` ES-module export from each\nlanguage's `parser.js` already returns a `variadic_inputs: [...]`\narray — names of parameters that the language considers\nvariadic. The inspector consumes that list at render time:\n\n- A port whose name is in `variadic_inputs` → the `var` button\n  renders as today (toggleable; the user can collapse the group\n  if they want).\n- A port whose name is NOT in `variadic_inputs` → the `var`\n  button is hidden (or disabled with a tooltip explaining why),\n  so the user cannot wire a five-slot variadic group into a\n  function that only accepts one positional arg.\n- Pre-existing maps that already carry a non-variadic-in-source\n  variadic group: validator surfaces them as an error when the\n  Compile button (issue 309) runs, same shape as 230's binding\n  errors. The user fixes by collapsing the group.\n\n### Implementation steps (post-231)\n\n1. `assets/js/004-inspector.js::mk_port_display` — when the\n   current box is a `call` box with a `ref`, ask the parser\n   module for the function's signature (cache per-box) and\n   decide whether to render the `var` button per the rules\n   above.\n2. New graph-level check in `src/001-schema.lua` (or wherever\n   231 puts the per-language signature lookup): for every box\n   in `variadic_inputs`, the parsed signature must agree.\n   Mismatches → errors in the same list `check_input_bindings`\n   uses.\n3. CLI mirror in `src/002-validate-map.lua` so the\n   command-line validator catches drift too.\n\n### Why it sits here and not in 231\n\n231's scope is one mechanical move — pull `parse_lua` /\n`parse_bash` out of the file browser into per-language ES\nmodules. Adding the variadic-correctness consequence to 231\nwould conflate the relocation with new behavior. Keeping the\nbehavior on 217 — the issue that introduced the variadic\nmechanic — means a reader following the variadic story finds\nboth the original feature and the eventual correctness check\nin the same file. 231 stays focused on relocation; 217 records\nthe consequence of relocation.\n\n---\n\n## Implementation notes (Part A, B — shipped)",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/completed/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md"
        }

That destination is issue 231 (move signature\nparsers into `langs/<name>/parser.js`).\n\n### Behavior after 231 lands\n\nThe `parse_function_signature` ES-module export from each\nlanguage's `parser.js` already returns a `variadic_inputs: [...]`\narray — names of parameters that the language considers\nvariadic. The inspector consumes that list at render time:\n\n- A port whose name is in `variadic_inputs` → the `var` button\n  renders as today (toggleable; the user can collapse the group\n  if they want).\n- A port whose name is NOT in `variadic_inputs` → the `var`\n  button is hidden (or disabled with a tooltip explaining why),\n  so the user cannot wire a five-slot variadic group into a\n  function that only accepts one positional arg.\n- Pre-existing maps that already carry a non-variadic-in-source\n  variadic group: validator surfaces them as an error when the\n  Compile button (issue 309) runs, same shape as 230's binding\n  errors. The user fixes by collapsing the group.\n\n### Implementation steps (post-231)\n\n1. `assets/js/004-inspector.js::mk_port_display` — when the\n   current box is a `call` box with a `ref`, ask the parser\n   module for the function's signature (cache per-box) and\n   decide whether to render the `var` button per the rules\n   above.\n2. New graph-level check in `src/001-schema.lua` (or wherever\n   231 puts the per-language signature lookup): for every box\n   in `variadic_inputs`, the parsed signature must agree.\n   Mismatches → errors in the same list `check_input_bindings`\n   uses.\n3. CLI mirror in `src/002-validate-map.lua` so the\n   command-line validator catches drift too.\n\n### Why it sits here and not in 231\n\n231's scope is one mechanical move — pull `parse_lua` /\n`parse_bash` out of the file browser into per-language ES\nmodules. Adding the variadic-correctness consequence to 231\nwould conflate the relocation with new behavior. Keeping the\nbehavior on 217 — the issue that introduced the variadic\nmechanic — means a reader following the variadic story finds\nboth the original feature and the eventual correctness check\nin the same file. 231 stays focused on relocation; 217 records\nthe consequence of relocation.\n\n---\n\n## Implementation notes (Part A, B — shipped)",

          "content":"// langs/bash/parser.js — Bash signature parser for the editor's file\n// browser. Issue 231 moved this code out of assets/js/007-filebrowser.js\n// so per-language knowledge lives next to the rest of each language's\n// pieces (spec.c, Makefile, lexer.js).\n\n// {{{ parse_inputs\n// Counts positional args a function references and names them after\n// any `local var=\"$N\"` assignments. Falls back to generic `argN` when\n// no local binding is found. Returns an array sized to the highest\n// `$N` the function touches.\nfunction parse_inputs(body) {\n  const params = {};\n  const local_re = /local\\s+(\\w+)\\s*=\\s*[\"']?\\$\\{?(\\d+)\\}?[\"']?/g;\n  let m;\n  while ((m = local_re.exec(body)) !== null) {\n    params[parseInt(m[2])] = m[1];\n  }\n  if (Object.keys(params).length > 0) {\n    const max = Math.max(...Object.keys(params).map(Number));\n    return Array.from({ length: max }, (_, i) => params[i + 1] || `arg${i + 1}`);\n  }\n  const seen = new Set();\n  const pos_re = /\\$\\{?(\\d+)\\}?/g;\n  while ((m = pos_re.exec(body)) !== null) {\n    const n = parseInt(m[1]);\n    if (n > 0) seen.add(n);\n  }\n  if (seen.size > 0) {\n    const max = Math.max(...seen);\n    return Array.from({ length: max }, (_, i) => `arg${i + 1}`);\n  }\n  return [];\n}\n// }}}\n\n// {{{ parse_functions\n// Returns [{name, inputs, outputs, variadic_tail}] for every shell\n// function declared in the file.\n//\n// Output is always a single named port `output` — Bash functions emit\n// one value via stdout (issue 218's single-output rule).\n//\n// `variadic_tail` is true when the function references `\"$@\"` or\n// bare `$@` after the named-positional region. Issue 217 part C uses\n// this to gate the editor's `var` toggle: a function that doesn't\n// touch `$@` shouldn't accept variadic input from the editor.\nexport function parse_functions(content) {\n  const fns  = [];\n  const re   = /^(\\w+)\\s*\\(\\s*\\)\\s*\\{/mg;\n  const skip = new Set(['if','while','for','case','do','done','fi','then','else']);\n  let m;\n  while ((m = re.exec(content)) !== null) {\n    const name = m[1];\n    if (skip.has(name)) continue;\n    const body_start = m.index + m[0].length;\n    const close      = content.indexOf('\\n}', body_start);\n    const body       = content.slice(body_start, close > -1 ? close : body_start + 800);\n    const inputs     = parse_inputs(body);\n    const variadic_tail = /\\$@|\\$\\{@\\}|\"\\$@\"/.test(body);\n    fns.push({ name, inputs, outputs: ['output'], variadic_tail });\n  }\n  return fns;\n}\n// }}}\n",

    "content":"// langs/bash/parser.js — Bash signature parser for the editor's file\n// browser. Issue 231 moved this code out of assets/js/007-filebrowser.js\n// so per-language knowledge lives next to the rest of each language's\n// pieces (spec.c, Makefile, lexer.js).\n\n// {{{ parse_inputs\n// Counts positional args a function references and names them after\n// any `local var=\"$N\"` assignments. Falls back to generic `argN` when\n// no local binding is found. Returns an array sized to the highest\n// `$N` the function touches.\nfunction parse_inputs(body) {\n  const params = {};\n  const local_re = /local\\s+(\\w+)\\s*=\\s*[\"']?\\$\\{?(\\d+)\\}?[\"']?/g;\n  let m;\n  while ((m = local_re.exec(body)) !== null) {\n    params[parseInt(m[2])] = m[1];\n  }\n  if (Object.keys(params).length > 0) {\n    const max = Math.max(...Object.keys(params).map(Number));\n    return Array.from({ length: max }, (_, i) => params[i + 1] || `arg${i + 1}`);\n  }\n  const seen = new Set();\n  const pos_re = /\\$\\{?(\\d+)\\}?/g;\n  while ((m = pos_re.exec(body)) !== null) {\n    const n = parseInt(m[1]);\n    if (n > 0) seen.add(n);\n  }\n  if (seen.size > 0) {\n    const max = Math.max(...seen);\n    return Array.from({ length: max }, (_, i) => `arg${i + 1}`);\n  }\n  return [];\n}\n// }}}\n\n// {{{ parse_functions\n// Returns [{name, inputs, outputs, variadic_tail}] for every shell\n// function declared in the file.\n//\n// Output is always a single named port `output` — Bash functions emit\n// one value via stdout (issue 218's single-output rule).\n//\n// `variadic_tail` is true when the function references `\"$@\"` or\n// bare `$@` after the named-positional region. Issue 217 part C uses\n// this to gate the editor's `var` toggle: a function that doesn't\n// touch `$@` shouldn't accept variadic input from the editor.\nexport function parse_functions(content) {\n  const fns  = [];\n  const re   = /^(\\w+)\\s*\\(\\s*\\)\\s*\\{/mg;\n  const skip = new Set(['if','while','for','case','do','done','fi','then','else']);\n  let m;\n  while ((m = re.exec(content)) !== null) {\n    const name = m[1];\n    if (skip.has(name)) continue;\n    const body_start = m.index + m[0].length;\n    const close      = content.indexOf('\\n}', body_start);\n    const body       = content.slice(body_start, close > -1 ? close : body_start + 800);\n    const inputs     = parse_inputs(body);\n    const variadic_tail = /\\$@|\\$\\{@\\}|\"\\$@\"/.test(body);\n    fns.push({ name, inputs, outputs: ['output'], variadic_tail });\n  }\n  return fns;\n}\n// }}}\n",

\"result\"\n          names.add('result');\n        }\n        // multi-value complex expression with no bare names: skip\n      });\n    }\n    return [...names];\n  }\n  // }}}\n\n  // {{{ parse_lua\n  function parse_lua(content) {\n    const fns    = [];\n    const fn_re  = /^function\\s+M\\.(\\w+)\\s*\\(([^)]*)\\)/mg;\n    let m;\n    while ((m = fn_re.exec(content)) !== null) {\n      const body_start = m.index + m[0].length;\n      const body_end   = lua_fn_end(content, body_start);\n      const body       = content.slice(body_start, body_end);\n      const inputs     = m[2].trim()\n        ? m[2].split(',').map(s => s.trim()).filter(Boolean)\n        : [];\n      const outputs    = parse_lua_returns(body);\n      fns.push({ name: m[1], inputs, outputs });\n    }\n    return fns;\n  }\n  // }}}\n\n  // {{{ parse_bash_inputs\n  function parse_bash_inputs(body) {\n    const params = {};\n    // local var=\"${N}\" or local var=\"$N\"\n    const local_re = /local\\s+(\\w+)\\s*=\\s*[\"']?\\$\\{?(\\d+)\\}?[\"']?/g;\n    let m;\n    while ((m = local_re.exec(body)) !== null) {\n      params[parseInt(m[2])] = m[1];\n    }\n    if (Object.keys(params).length > 0) {\n      const max = Math.max(...Object.keys(params).map(Number));\n      return Array.from({ length: max }, (_, i) => params[i + 1] || `arg${i + 1}`);\n    }\n    // fall back: scan for raw $N references\n    const seen = new Set();\n    const pos_re = /\\$\\{?(\\d+)\\}?/g;\n    while ((m = pos_re.exec(body)) !== null) {\n      const n = parseInt(m[1]);\n      if (n > 0) seen.add(n);\n    }\n    if (seen.size > 0) {\n      const max = Math.max(...seen);\n      return Array.from({ length: max }, (_, i) => `arg${i + 1}`);\n    }\n    return [];\n  }\n  // }}}\n\n  // {{{ parse_bash\n  function parse_bash(content) {\n    const fns   = [];\n    const re    = /^(\\w+)\\s*\\(\\s*\\)\\s*\\{/mg;\n    const skip  = new Set(['if','while','for','case','do','done','fi','then','else']);\n    let m;\n    while ((m = re.exec(content)) !== null) {\n      const name = m[1];\n      if (skip.has(name)) continue;\n      const body_start = m.index + m[0].length;\n      const close      = content.indexOf('\\n}', body_start);\n      const body       = content.slice(body_start, close > -1 ? close : body_start + 800);\n      const inputs     = parse_bash_inputs(body);\n      fns.push({ name, inputs, outputs: ['output'] });\n    }\n    return fns;\n  }\n  // }}}\n\n  // {{{ parse_functions\n  // Returns [{name, inputs:[string], outputs:[string]}] for a given file.\n  function parse_functions(content, filename) {\n    const ext = filename.split('.').pop();\n    if (ext === 'lua') return parse_lua(content);\n    if (ext === 'sh')  return parse_bash(content);\n    return null;  // null = no parser for this extension\n  }\n  // }}}",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"// Source file browser and function signature parser.\n// Renders into the inspector panel: file list → function list → auto-populate box ports.\n\nconst FileBrowser = (() => {\n\n  // {{{ Parser registry (issue 231)\n  // Lazy-loads a per-language signature parser the first time a file\n  // of that language is opened. Cached afterwards. Files with an\n  // unknown extension or a missing parser fall back to \"no parser\n  // available\" — the file is listed but offers no function picker.\n  // Same lazy-import shape as the lexer registry in 008-source-view.js.\n  const EXT_TO_LANG = { lua: 'lua', sh: 'bash', bash: 'bash' };\n  const parser_cache = {};   // lang_name → { parse_functions } | null\n\n  async function load_parser(lang) {\n    if (lang in parser_cache) return parser_cache[lang];\n    try {\n      const mod = await import('/langs/' + lang + '/parser.js');\n      parser_cache[lang] = mod;\n      return mod;\n    } catch (e) {\n      console.warn('no parser for ' + lang + ':', e.message);\n      parser_cache[lang] = null;\n      return null;\n    }\n  }\n  // }}}\n\n  // {{{ parse_functions\n  // Returns [{name, inputs, outputs, variadic_tail}] for the file's\n  // public functions, or null when no parser is available for the\n  // extension. Per-language detail lives in langs/<name>/parser.js;\n  // this function just dispatches.\n  async function parse_functions(content, filename) {\n    const ext  = (filename || '').split('.').pop();\n    const lang = EXT_TO_LANG[ext];\n    if (!lang) return null;\n    const mod = await load_parser(lang);\n    if (!mod || typeof mod.parse_functions !== 'function') return null;\n    try {\n      return mod.parse_functions(content);\n    } catch (e) {\n      console.warn('parser error for ' + filename + ':', e.message);\n      return null;\n    }\n  }\n  // }}}",
